Tech Report: These Are the Best Ways to Encrypt Your Email

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, you probably already know that your email isn't actually all that private, especially if you have a free account with a major service provider like Gmail (Google) or Outlook (Microsoft).
  • Recent findings suggest that as this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server.
  • In a recent development, emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, you probably already know that your email isn't actually all that private, especially if you have a free account with a major service provider like Gmail (Google) or Outlook (Microsoft). But if you are sending sensitive information via email, you can minimize what can be snooped on and by whom using end-to-end encryption, which generally ensures that only the recipient can read your message. Here's what you need to know about email encryption and how to set up an extra layer of privacy.

Recent findings suggest that as this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server. However, encryption is temporarily stripped at each server: content is received and processed in plaintext and then re-encrypted when it leaves, meaning it could be read, logged, and distributed by the server provider.

In a recent development, emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox. But this only prevents someone with physical access to the server hardware from reading messages, as Google still holds the encryption key and can access stored data. And, as PCMag points out, Google is scanning your messages to a degree, and it (along with other email providers) can and will hand emails over to law enforcement and government agencies in some cases.

Sources indicate that by contrast, with end-to-end encryption (E2EE), emails are readable only on the sender's and recipient's devices, and can be decrypted only with the recipient's private key. They're never translated into plaintext as they pass between and through servers to their destination, meaning that no one—including server providers, hackers, or law enforcement—can view the content. It's worth noting, though, that E2EE is not impenetrable nor a total guarantee of privacy. For example, metadata like subject lines and email addresses may remain in plaintext, and encrypted messages are still susceptible to phishing. Plus, forwarding an encrypted message breaks the encryption.

Still, end-to-end encryption is especially useful when sending sensitive information that may be valuable to bad actors, though if security and privacy are a high priority, you may want to consider it for all of your emails. How you deploy encryption depends on whether you are adding it to your current email or switching to a dedicated provider.

If you have an account with a major email provider like Gmail, Outlook, or Apple Mail, you can add a third-party tool that layers an encryption protocol like OpenPGP on top of your existing account. PCMag recommends PreVeil, SecureMyEmail, and Virtru (which is limited to Gmail people in Chrome) for those who want to keep their current emails. Mailvelope is a browser add-on (and therefore a desktop-only tool) available in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, though it can also be installed on other browsers, like Brave, that are built on the same architecture. FlowCrypt integrates with Gmail and Google Workspace on desktop and mobile.

Note that enterprise consumers of Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 have access to true end-to-end encryption without third-party add-ons. Gmail's Confidential mode and Outlook's Encrypt feature, available to all users, are not E2EE equivalents, as Google and Microsoft, respectively, still manage the keys.

It has been revealed that for those who are willing to start fresh with a new email address (or who have a custom domain), providers like Proton Mail or Tuta offer native end-to-end encryption. The caveat: by default, this is only between consumers on the same service, so from one Proton user to another. If you want to send an end-to-end encrypted email from Proton to a Gmail user, for example, you have to set up password protection (and share the password via another secure channel) or use a PGP-compatible tool like those listed above. You can also Proton's Gmail integration does allow for end-to-end encryption, but only if both Gmail parties are using the Proton integration.

Sources indicate that the bottom line here is that email wasn't designed to be a highly secure form of communication. End-to-end encryption does add a layer of privacy and security if you jump through hoops to set it up, but it's still susceptible to human error and social engineering.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • "The Lion King" is the crowning achievement of the Disney Renaissance.
  • Recent findings suggest that directed by Roger Allers and Rob Minkoff, "Lion King" was the highest grossing film of 1994 and, at the time, the second highest grossing film in history (earning more than $770 million during its initial release).
  • Recent findings suggest that the 1998 sequel, "The Lion King II: Simba's Pride," is pretty good as far as direct-to-video Disney sequels go.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"The Lion King" is the crowning achievement of the Disney Renaissance. If you were born after, say, 1989, then the movie was almost certainly a cornerstone of your childhood. That makes it amusing to look back and realize Disney didn't expect "The Lion King" to be one of the studio's greatest works.

Recent findings suggest that directed by Roger Allers and Rob Minkoff, "Lion King" was the highest grossing film of 1994 and, at the time, the second highest grossing film in history (earning more than $770 million during its initial release). More than any other animated Disney classic, "The Lion King" is a franchise unto itself — it's even been adapted as a Broadway play.

Recent findings suggest that the 1998 sequel, "The Lion King II: Simba's Pride," is pretty good as far as direct-to-video Disney sequels go. Scene-stealing comic relief, and Simba's foster fathers, Timon & Pumbaa (Nathan Lane & Ernie Sabella, whose audition changed the movie), got their own TV show and spin-off movie "The Lion King 1 ½." Disney Jr. aired a sequel TV series, "The Lion Guard," and in 2019, Disney produced a photorealistic "Lion King" remake that got its own prequel, "Mufasa." Granted, that remake only proved how special the original and its luscious cartooning is.

An essential part of the majesty of "The Lion King" is the movie's sound. Hans Zimmer's Oscar-winning score, plus songs composed by Elton John with lyrics by Tim Rice. Even if you don't speak the Zulu language, who can't recall the opening "Circle of Life" song as all of the savannah marches to pride rock to pay tribute to newly introduced prince Simba (Jonathan Taylor Thomas)? Then there's the voice acting, especially the late James Earl Jones as Simba's father Mufasa — no voice in cinema history better feels like a real father and a king all at once.

Recent findings suggest that mufasa is murdered early on in "The Lion King" by his envious brother Scar (Jeremy Irons) staging a wildebeest stampede to trap Simba. (This complex sequence took three years to animate properly.) Simba, convinced by Scar it's all his fault, runs away in shame and spends years living in exile, learning "Hakuna Matata" (It means no worries!) from Timon and Pumbaa. When his childhood friend Nala (Moira Kelly) comes knocking, the grown Simba (Matthew Broderick) has to finally face his past.

Sources indicate that with help from mandrill shaman Rafiki (Robert Guillaume), that's what Simba does. Mufasa once told Simba to look up into the sky to remember his father would always be with him. Mufasa literally manifests in the clouds, pushing Simba to fulfill his birthright: "Remember who you are. You are my son and the one true king.".

According to recent reports, "The Lion King" is often called a kid-friendly staging of "Hamlet" with talking animals. This scene mirrors the ghost of Hamlet's murdered father talking to his son. But James Earl Jones' voice is so grand that it feels more like God speaking to Christ.

According to recent reports, yet the scene also unfurls common criticism of "The Lion King" for its themes and political subtext. Textually, "The Lion King" is a pro-monarchy movie. It is quite literally about how the restoration of the proper heir to the throne heals the world. (The movie stacks the deck by making Scar a lazy and ill-equipped king on top of him being a kinslayer.) Mufasa frames Simba as the rightful king simply because he's the son of a king, suggesting (to quote Princess Azula of "Avatar: The Last Airbender") that "the divine right to rule is something you're born with." Pretty regressive attitude for the 1990s, but it's undeniably epic storytelling, too.

Sources indicate that "The Lion King" is filled with memorable quotes and song lyrics from its ensemble, so let's narrow that and list only Mufasa's greatest lines. Besides the inimitable power of James Earl Jones' voice, Mufasa's limited screentime — most of it spent schooling or bond with his son — makes every bit of his dialogue feels special.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the greatest things about showrunners Ashley Lyle and Bart Nickerson’s psychological horror show Yellowjackets is that you never know what bananas shenanigans will happen next. We’re only one episode into Yellowjackets season 4, and we’re happy to report that this still holds true, with a cliffhanger ending that will leave you wondering what the hell just happened.

It has been revealed that at the end of season 3, teen Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) had just managed to contact someone outside the remote wilderness using the satellite phone they’d recovered from the scientific expedition that had recently discovered them. Back at the camp, teen Shauna (Sophie Nélisse), now in charge, is furious at Natalie for calling for help behind her back.

This article contains spoilers for Yellowjackets season 4 episode 1, “Hivemind.”.

It was established in the first season of Yellowjackets that the girls (and Travis) would eventually be rescued, as the time jumps between 2021 and 1996 make clear. However, the mystery was more about how that would happen and what the consequences of the Yellowjackets' rescue would be.

In “Hivemind,” the outcome of that phone call is made pretty clear. The girls and Travis are rescued and brought to a hospital in Canada, though several are missing, including poor Mari Ibarra (Alexa Barajas), who ended up being skewered in the same pit she was previously rescued from during one of the girls’ cannibalistic hunts in season 3. This leads to a few emotional scenes of the parents of the dead breaking down and the survivors exchanging agonizingly guilty looks.

Industry observers note that at first, it looks like we’ll skip the immediate fallout as the rest of the Yellowjackets learn about Natalie’s call for help. Most of “Hivemind” in the teen timeline focuses on the reunion between the parents and survivors, and the teens’ efforts to cover up the deplorable things they did in the wilderness by lying to the ranger and therapist who question them.

In a recent development, that is, until the end of the episode, when the story jumps back to the wilderness, before the rescue. We see Natalie stumble back into camp, wide-eyed and terrified. She then asks a question that I too say at the end of every Yellowjackets episode: “What the fuck?”.

Yellowjackets’ first episode may have ended on a truly diabolical cliffhanger, but that doesn’t mean we don’t have clues about what Natalie saw to make her react with so much shock.

Sources indicate that for one thing, the opening credits and teaser trailers for the fourth season have shown clips of teen Shauna looking battered and beaten. We know, based on the snow surrounding Shauna in this scene, that unless there is a time skip, her looking this way is likely to take place during the Yellowjackets' time in the wilderness.

Recent findings suggest that what reason would the girls have to attack Shauna? A lot. Unlike Tai (Jasmin Savoy Brown), who wants to conceal the cannibalism and murders the girls committed during their time there, and Lottie (Courtney Eaton), who genuinely believes she has a spiritual connection to the wilderness’s supernatural goings-on, Shauna’s reason for staying in the wilderness is pretty damn selfish: she enjoys the power and hedonism that wilderness life encourages.

Her desire to be the alpha of this pack of wolves in girls’ clothing has, unfortunately, made her an easy target for the others’ hatred. While most of the girls want to go home, Shauna refuses to let them and has even trained a gun on some of her fellow Yellowjackets, including her situationship, Melissa (Jenna Burgess).

Sources indicate that if all the girls have turned on Shauna and left her in a bad way, Natalie could be reacting to that. After all, the first episode does show that teen Shauna has several scars and bruises on her face in the hospital, that weren’t there when we saw Shauna at the end of season 3.

That being said, we do know a handful of the girls don’t make it back to civilization — including the lone science researcher Hannah (Ashley Sutton), who murdered one of her own last season in a bid to be accepted by the teens. That appealed to Shauna for a little while, but given how volatile Shauna is about being rescued, and how little they know about Hannah, it's also likely that Natalie has seen Shauna and the others turn on Hannah as a consequence of Natalie’s call for help.

What Natalie has seen likely won’t be confirmed until next week. Even so, Yellowjackets likes to surprise its audience, and we wouldn’t be shocked if something we haven’t speculated about has turned up at camp, making the arrival of people searching for the Yellowjackets even more precarious.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

10 Privacy Hacks Every Mac User Should Know

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1066 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple has a pretty good track record on privacy.
  • According to recent reports, enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device.
  • It has been revealed that another hack for maintaining privacy on public networks is to enable rotating MAC addresses, which randomizes the identifier your device broadcasts when scanning for and connecting to wifi.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple has a pretty good track record on privacy. The company bakes a number of protections into its OSes to keep your data from being shared or stolen. That said, you can make your Apple devices even more secure. There are plenty of opt-in settings that make it even harder for anyone to snoop on your device and activity. These are the best privacy hacks for your Mac.

According to recent reports, enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device. Turning on Stealth Mode prevents your Mac from even responding to these requests, essentially making it invisible to anything that's scanning a network you're connected to. This makes it more difficult for hackers and malware to know your device exists, much less attack it. This can interfere with certain essential activity when you're on your home network, but it's a valuable security setting when on public wifi. You can leave Firewall on all the time and enable Stealth Mode only as needed. Go to Settings > Network > Firewall, flip the toggle, then hit Options to manage Stealth Mode.

It has been revealed that another hack for maintaining privacy on public networks is to enable rotating MAC addresses, which randomizes the identifier your device broadcasts when scanning for and connecting to wifi. If you use either your real MAC address or a fixed one (random but unchanging), it's easier to track your activity on that network, including when you arrive, how long you stay, and when you leave. Rotating addresses are best for public, shared networks you temporarily connect to, and don't require a login via a captive portal (like hotel wifi). You can turn this on for specific networks via Settings > Wi-Fi > [Network Name] > Details and change Private Wi-Fi address to Rotating.

It has been revealed that images and screenshots contain metadata, such as timestamps, device and hardware details, and, in the case of photos, physical location. Much of this information is stripped automatically when you share files to social media or via encrypted messaging apps, but if you're sending them via text or email, posting to forums, or sharing over AirDrop, metadata remains intact. You can easily remove metadata from your images right on your desktop. Select the file and hit control + click to bring up an options menu, then go to Quick Actions > Convert Image. Uncheck the box next to Preserve Metadata, then hit Convert. (This is also useful for quickly converting HEIC to JPEG without opening a separate app.).

Recent findings suggest that apple collects information about your device for diagnostic purposes or to improve apps and services, some of which is shared with third-party app developers. This may include crash and usage data as well as recordings and transcripts of Siri interactions and iCloud analytics. You can disable sharing for some or all of these categories under Settings > Privacy & Security > Analytics & Improvements.

Industry observers note that you may be surprised by the number of apps and system services that use your device's location in the background. You should definitely disable location services for third-party apps that don't require location to function. You can find these toggles under Settings > Privacy & Security > Location Services. You can also turn off location permissions for some Apple apps and services if you're not using them on your device, like Weather and Maps. Finally, tap System Services and disable location for any non-essential features—at the very least, disable "Mac Analytics" and "Significant Locations & routes" (which lets your Mac and other iCloud devices learn locations and routes you use often).

Industry observers note that third-party apps on your Mac that need access to your device's camera and microphone have to request permission, and it's easy to grant this in the moment and then forget that you've allowed it. You should regularly audit which apps have these permissions and revoke access from those that don't need them on a day-to-day basis. Disabling them forces the app to ask again. Go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Microphone or Camera to see the allowed apps and flip the toggle to disable permissions.

Another permission type you may have granted without much thought is local network access. This allows third-party apps to discover and communicate with other devices—printers, smart speakers, and IoT devices—on your home wifi. While this may be useful for services like Spotify that cast to connected hardware, other utilities, media apps, and games probably don't need to be mapping your network in the background. Go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Local Network to audit permissions and disable those that aren't needed.

According to recent reports, another notable permission to check concerns third-party apps that have access to your Mac's full disk, which includes data from Mail, Messages, Safari, Home, Time Machine, and admin settings. If an app only works with files you explicitly open and save, it doesn't need full disk access. Legitimate use cases may include antivirus and malware scanners, productivity tools, or backup utilities that you trust. You can also audit which apps have access to specific files and folders. This is under Settings > Privacy & Security > Full Disk Access or Files & Folders.

Recent findings suggest that if you're using iCloud to store photos, files, and device backups, your data is encrypted on Apple's servers and in transit. Apple still holds the decryption key, which is useful if you somehow get locked out of your account and need help recovering it, but for sensitive data—including device backups—end-to-end encryption is the most secure way to ensure no one but you can gain access. Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in setting for iCloud that encrypts your information end to end. You'll need to set up an alternative recovery method, such as your device passcode with two-factor authentication, a recovery contact, or a recovery key. Be careful, though: If you lose access to this recovery method, you will lose your data. You can enable Advanced Data Protection on your Mac under System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Advanced Data Protection > Turn On. Note that some iCloud data, including passwords and payment methods, are already end-to-end encrypted by default.

Sources indicate that when Francis Lawrence, the filmmaker behind The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, greets me over Zoom, he’s aware that his darkly lit, gothic backdrop makes him look a bit like the villainous President Snow. “All I need is a significant eagle back here,” the white-haired, smartly dressed director jokes.

Sources indicate that lawrence has helmed almost every film in Lionsgate’s blockbuster series, based on Suzanne Collins’s best-selling novels about a dystopia where a bloodthirsty dictator forces children to fight to the death for the elite’s entertainment. He joined the franchise for its 2013 sequel, Catching Fire, and has directed only three non–Hunger Games movies in the decade-plus since. In that time, one could argue, the world has tilted further toward the oppressive future depicted in Collins’s novels—see, for instance, Donald Trump’s Hunger Games–esque Patriot Games. And while Lawrence isn’t naming names, he’s never lost sight of the movies’ larger political message. “I feel really lucky to be able to tell stories that matter, that are wrapped in these commercial packages,” he tells Vanity Fair. “So anytime one of these things comes around, I jump at it.”.

Just as the original Hunger Games film made a star of Oscar winner Jennifer Lawrence (who returns for a scene in the new movie), Sunrise on the Reaping introduces the world to Australian newcomer Joseph Zada. He plays the younger version of Woody Harrelson’s Haymitch Abernathy, a victor of the Hunger Games who later serves as a mentor to actor Lawrence’s Katniss Everdeen. Making a reflective movie prompted director Lawrence to reflect on his own Hollywood trajectory. “The biggest difference is that I’m a lot more relaxed. I was nervous as hell on Catching Fire,” he indicates. “It was my fourth movie. It was a movie I was inheriting. It was a big movie, and it was a massive cast. So I was really intimidated. Now I have much more fun, I will say. I’m much more comfortable with actors, and the amount of actors, and with logistics. And there’s definitely a family that’s built into it, which is very key for me. There’s, what, 14 years of my life spent making these movies? So it has to be fun.”.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: When did you become aware of Sunrise on the Reaping, and at what point did you and Suzanne Collins start discussing an adaptation?

According to recent reports, francis Lawrence: When we did the original series of movies, and we finished the last Mockingjay, she stated she was done, and we thought that was it. Then she surprised me and Nina [Jacobson], the producer, with Ballad, however many years later. And she never tells us when she’s writing. Even when she has something to read, she never tells us what it’s about. She’s very superstitious about it all. So we got the call, which was very exciting. And she said, “Go to my agent’s house. There’s a manuscript. Let’s talk after you read it.”.

According to recent reports, I got to his house, sat in his backyard, and there was a manuscript and a copy of Catching Fire sitting on top of it with a few tabs in it. I opened to the tabs and saw that it had the portion where Katniss and Peeta were looking up the Haymitch Games, that sequence from the book. And I was like, Oh, she’s written the Haymitch story, which was very exciting. And that started the process that we always have, which is that I read the manuscript in one sitting, then read it a second time after having a conversation with Suzanne.

Then I fly to New York and meet her at Scholastic, and we sit up in a conference room for about a week going through the book, beat by beat, of what we think the movie is going to be. She and I lay it all out and chat, and she sits on her computer and writes a scriptment. Then that’s the thing that we turn over to the screenwriter.

How have you built that trust with the author of these books, having adapted them for more than a decade now?

In a recent development, that working process happened accidentally when I signed on to do Catching Fire. I had never done a sequel to someone else’s first movie before. And when Lionsgate and the first director, [Gary Ross], parted ways and I got the call, they didn’t have a script, but they had started the process of developing it before I was on board. And so I signed on based on the book and had planned a trip to Newly introduced York to meet with Suzanne.

The script came on the day that I was traveling to Newly introduced York. I read it, and it was not the movie that I wanted to make—because I loved the book, and it was not the book. Luckily, nobody else wanted to make that version of the movie either. Our meeting of me just picking her brain turned into, “This script doesn’t work. Let’s go through, page by page, and figure out the version of the movie we want to make.”.

Industry observers note that that’s what really formed the bond—just working really, really closely with her. Spending 8 or 10 hours a day for a week or two in a conference room—me riffing on visual ideas and her talking about the story. We think the same way in terms of storytelling, structure, and she seemed to take to my visual ideas.

Sources indicate that there’s this weird dynamic that happens as we get closer to production. We’re usually developing the script pretty much within a week of shooting. But the production is also building. So you have thousands of people working, figuring out locations, traveling in different parts of the world. The stress levels are building.

Recent findings suggest that suzanne and I have related the relationship to almost like a mother-son relationship. It starts really lovely and creative, but then as we get closer and closer, it’s me being that late teen who’s ready to leave the home, like, Okay, enough’s enough. I’m going to go make the movie now. I have to say, I love the process. It’s not without its stress sometimes, but that’s part of the closeness of it all that I cherish.

How did this film’s futuristic-meets-1970s aesthetic come about?

According to recent reports, there was an element [of the story] that reminded me a bit of Alice in Wonderland, which then made me think of Jefferson Airplane, that song “White Rabbit,” which brought me to the ’60s and ’70s. Then you can look at characters certain ways. Like, Haymitch, you go, Okay, he’s from, like, young Bruce Springsteen, or Lenore Dove [played by Whitney Peak], like a young Stevie Nicks. And you get this hippie vibe. And the Capitol is that Warhol Studio 54 crowd, and Snow like a ’70s Yves Saint Laurent.

How do you go about casting a young Haymitch, finding an actor who can anchor the film like Jennifer Lawrence did in the original Hunger Games film?

Our casting director, Deb Zane, had met him, and I want to say before he did East of Eden. She had a lot of faith in him. We liked his self-tape a lot. But we knew that he was going to have to pull a lot off. He starts as a very optimistic, fun, playful, young guy in love, and in this movie has to turn into somebody that’s much closer to the Haymitch that we’re used to—cynical and a drunk. He’s going to have to go through a lot of emotional trauma, plus have that kind of mischievousness, irreverence, all these different elements that Woody [Harrelson] has naturally. And so we really put him through the ringer. We did a lot of tests, kept bringing him back, bringing him back, bringing him back. He and I were modulating how much Woody we feel in his performance.

According to recent reports, I want to make sure that everybody makes the role their own. That they find the spirit of the character and that it’s not trying to do an imitation of somebody. That’s true of Elle [Fanning] doing Effie, of Ralph [Fiennes] doing Snow, of Jesse [Plemons] doing Plutarch, Kieran [Culkin] as Caesar. Everybody has to figure out how to do it on their own. Then the weird thing is that Kelvin [Harrison Jr., who plays a young Beetee], has worked with Jeffrey [Wright] three times. So he’s fairly close with Jeffrey. When he got the role, he called and stated, “You won’t believe this, but I’m actually playing the young version of you.” He could just conjure Jeffrey Wright. His voice, the speech patterns, the timbre of the sound of everything. It was pretty wild.

It has been revealed that were there storylines from the previous films that you felt you could plant Easter eggs for? I’m thinking specifically of the romantic chemistry between Effie and Haymitch.

Industry observers note that there are certain Capitol characters where I give a lot of freedom for improvisation. Effie, Caesar, Drusilla [played by Glenn Close], there’s a lot of room for ad-libs. One of the elements that we definitely played with a bit came from an improvised moment in the [last] Mockingjay. We were shooting this scene in Atlanta outside of Snow’s mansion, which is one of the very last scenes of Katniss in the Capitol. She’s saying goodbye to Effie, and then Haymitch and Effie kiss.

In a recent development, quite honestly, it was an idea because Woody just wanted to kiss Elizabeth Banks. But everybody thought it would be fun and that the fans would dig it, that Haymitch kissed her. Then it became this big thing of this hidden love that Haymitch and Effie have for one another. And Elle played into that a bit. So there’s, I would say, a hint of flirtation here between the two, less so on Haymitch’s side. His heart is obviously somewhere else in the story. But Elle definitely brought a bit of that to it. That was not scripted. That’s the fun of having great actors.

What was it like to reunite Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Woody Harrelson from the original movies?

It has been revealed that jen and I have stayed close over the years. We’ve done four movies together. Josh, who basically has moved to Spain, I haven’t seen in a long time. Woody I see off and on and text every once in a while. But there was something really special about the three of them being back together.

It’s also really, for the most part, the same crew from 2012, when we started making Catching Fire. It’s the same DP [Jo Willems], the same camera operator [David J. Thompson], the same AD [Christopher Surgent].

Industry observers note that [When] they got to the hotel, Jen and Josh were in the bar having a beer or something, and I was like, Okay, I won’t even shower. I won’t get out of my rain gear. I’ll just come in. The next thing you know, there were 40 of us who had been together since Catching Fire, the gang back together. It’s like a high school reunion or something, but in the best possible way.

There’s a futility to what happens in this film, knowing where we end up in future movies. How do you handle that aspect of history being doomed to repeat itself?

Look, we’re doing a story where you know the lead character is going to make it out. It’s really about how he makes it out, and what he ends up being like at the end of it all. What I’m really pleased about is that the way Suzanne wrote the book, and the way I think we’ve ended the movie, there is a sense of hope that the tragedy is not for nothing. That was really important to me. And one of the beautiful elements in the story, which comes a bit later, is this sense of, everybody has to find their voice. Everybody has to participate.

It really deals with this thing that I think is happening a lot today, where you find apathy: people not wanting to vote, feeling even if they do vote that it’s not going to matter. This idea that you have to be active, and you can’t expect immediate gratification—that everybody needs to stand up and it may take generations, but you still have to do it.

Outside of my screening on the Upper West Side, there was a group protesting Elon Musk and data centers because the documentary about him was playing at the theater. It was a reminder that there will always be something to rise up against, and always people who will be willing to do it.

Industry observers note that yeah, exactly. And ideally, at some point, if everybody stands up, something will change.

During the 13 years that you’ve worked in this universe, dystopia has felt more and more familiar. How have real-world events influenced your filmmaking?

Industry observers note that in the 56 years I’ve been alive, there’s never really been a time where I’ve felt like, Oh wow, everything is great. Nothing is wrong in the world. It always feels like there’s some dystopian sense about the world at any given time. And somehow Suzanne is always able to write these stories about it, which is what makes these movies feel timeless. A lot of people just see them as spectacles, but really they’re about our times very specifically. Almost in a subversive way, I feel like we’ve gotten to smuggle these ideas into these movies that a lot of people go see.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article contains spoilers for "Yellowjackets" Season 4 Episode 1 "Hivemind.".

The "Yellowjackets" Season 4 marketing campaign has leaned hard on Alanis Morissette's song "Ironic," featuring it in both trailers for the season. A bunch of teenagers stuck in the wilderness for months are finally rescued, but they're all unhappy to be going home for one reason or another? Yeah, that's about as ironic as rain on your wedding day.

The fourth and final season has debuted (read /Film's review here) and it jumps ahead from Season 3's cliffhanger ending when Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) got an SOS call out of the Wilderness. In "Hivemind," the survivors are recovering in a Canadian hospital and, about halfway through the episode, they reunite with their parents. This introduces us to Shauna's (Sophie Nélisse) mother (Gabrielle Miller, who definitely looks convincing as the mother of a woman who grows up to be Melanie Lynskey).

Besides her parents being divorced, "Yellowjackets" has given us precious little information about Shauna's childhood home life. The first stretch of Season 1 episodes offered glimpses into some of the Yellowjackets' earlier childhoods, but not Shauna's. That has generated lots of "Fellowjacket" fan speculation, from fanfiction to forum posts, about what Shauna's mom is like. Shauna is the lead in the "Yellowjackets" ensemble, and her arc begins with her feeling invisible (including next to her best friend) before she becomes a tyrant in the Wilderness.

Information on Shauna's parents has felt like a missing piece to her character, especially since motherhood is also an essential theme for both iterations of Shauna. She was pregnant, from her future husband Jeff, while stuck in the Wilderness. In "Yellowjackets" Season 2, she suffered a stillbirth, during which she slipped into an extremely lucid dream of her teammates cannibalizing her newborn son.

In a recent development, the death of Shauna's baby shapes every part of her life afterward, from her desire to make everyone else miserable in the 1990s timeline to how, in the present day story, she keeps her daughter Callie (Sarah Desjardins) at arm's length. (Season 3 episode "Them's The Brakes" features teen Shauna experiencing a vision of her son still alive. Scored like "Rosemary's Baby," it's also the only time in Season 3 that Shauna looks truly happy.).

Now, "Yellowjackets" Season 4 can complete the puzzle by showing Shauna's relationship with her own mother. We don't get much of Mrs. Shipman in this episode, granted, but she seems naturally relieved to see her daughter is still alive. (That automatically makes her a better parent than Natalie's mom, who doesn't even bother to show up.) Shauna spends most of the episode silent and scowling. When doctors notice her medical exams suggest she's given birth recently, she clams up and denies it. Her mother notices Shauna was talking with an OB/GYN, though, and appears to put the pieces together.

Industry observers note that "Hivemind" ends with the Yellowjackets and their parents on a plane back home to Upcoming Jersey, recreating a glimpse of their rescue seen in Season 2 premiere "Friends, Romans, Countrymen." At least some of the parents will be massive supporting players this season; you don't do stunt casting like Molly Ringwald as Van's (Liv Hewson) mother if she was just (barely) going to be in this one episode. So, how will the Shipman household readjust now that Shauna's back? We'll find out, but that's not the only lingering question about Shauna.

When we last saw Shauna at the end of Season 3, she was freshly crowned as the Antler Queen. In "Hivemind," her face is horribly bruised and swollen. How'd that happen?

"Hivemind" might have you thinking the show is going to skip over the Yellowjackets' final days in the Wilderness. Instead, "Yellowjackets" Season 4 breaks down the show's fractured timeline even further, because the lead-up to the girls' rescue and their first days back home are being told in parallel. The very last scene of "Hivemind" features Natalie, having just made the SOS call, running back to the Yellowjackets' camp and exclaiming "what the f***?" at the sight waiting for her there, promising the show has more story to tell of the Wilderness.

It has been revealed that at the very least, "Yellowjackets" Season 4 isn't repeating the major sin of Season 3. Season 2 ended with the Yellowjackets' cabin shelter burning down in the dead of winter. Then, Season 3 jumped over that cliffhanger months ahead to spring, where they'd already built latest shelter and had pulled back on their descent into cannibalism and ritual. Just like that, the show skipped past the roughest stretch of the team's survival.

It was too substantial a jump. "Hivemind" — which pointedly features the survivors staying silent as they're grilled about what happened during their time stranded — delights in keeping the audience in suspense, almost like it wants you to think the show is again resolving a cliffhanger by leaping past it. Is holding out too clever by half? Or is this the most efficient way to keep the show's Wilderness thrills until the end while also delivering long-awaited stories like the Yellowjackets reuniting with their parents?

"Yellowjackets" Season 4 is streaming on Paramount+, with new episodes dropping on Fridays.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updates are generally good for your devices. The latest Chrome update, for example, patches an actively exploited security vulnerability, while Apple's latest updates stop people from seeing iMessages they shouldn't have access to. In most cases, it's beneficial to update your tech to the latest software version whenever possible.

Industry observers note that sadly, updates aren't all perfect, as Google Pixel consumers are discovering this week. As reported by Android Authority, Google's November update apparently shipped with a bug that breaks some Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 cameras. Seeing as Pixels are rather famous for their shooters, this is a decidedly unfortunate glitch.

Here's the situation: Following the November patch, some consumers are opening their Pixel Camera apps to find an error that reads, "Something went wrong. Close and open the Camera app again," with a "Learn More" link to, well, learn more. Others aren't receiving the error, but are instead running into a blank Camera viewfinder, as if the lens is totally covered. What's more, some users are reportedly saying that the issue is present on third-party camera apps, not just the Pixel Camera app. That would imply this is an issue with the camera system-wide, not just the Pixel Camera app itself.

To be clear, it doesn't seem like this is a universal concern. It's not like all Pixel people are now running with broken cameras. But based on the forum complaints Android Authority discovered, it seems reasonable to assume that this glitch isn't limited to just a handful of unlucky Pixel owners.

Recent findings suggest that luckily, there is an apparent workaround here, though it's not totally obvious. Some consumers are having no luck restarting their Pixels, while others report that a factory reset wasn't enough to restore camera functionality.

According to recent reports, what does appear to work, however, is shutting your Pixel down and waiting five minutes or so. It's not clear why, but giving your Pixel a chance to "breathe" seems to shake the glitch and bring back your camera. As Android Authority reports, that fix comes from "Diamond and Gold product experts" on Google's Support forum.

If your Pixel's camera is giving you grief following the November revision, this workaround is definitely worth a try—especially since more drastic measures don't actually seem to do anything. As the issue does seem to be rather widespread, I wouldn't be surprised to see Google issue a patch in the coming days. But until then, turning your phone off for five minutes may be a decent compromise.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Makes One Huge Change From The Book

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stop reading if the thought of kids fighting to the death in the arena makes your stomach turn — this article contains major spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".

It's not a secret that, across the board, the Hunger Games franchise is dark and disturbing. Yet, the literary version of the 2025 prequel "Sunrise on the Reaping" somehow manages to make the books that came before it look like light-hearted fairytales, especially one plot point that may just be the most upsetting and depraved thing the Hunger Games property has ever done. Of course, in every literary and cinematic story set in this fictional universe, the titular games put actual children into dangerous arenas and force them to fight to the death, all while it's presented to the totalitarian regime of Panem and its captive citizens as televised entertainment. (Thankfully, the franchise does tend to center winners, so we don't have to watch all of our favorite characters killed in increasingly brutal ways.).

Sources indicate that in the massive screen adaptation of "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," every unsettling plot point appears in the movie, leading to some truly gutting moments as eventual victor Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) loses loved ones and allies. There's one notable difference from page to screen, though, and I can certainly understand why director Francis Lawrence made this tweak. The book is ... unrelentingly violent.

Again, some degree of violence is to be expected here if you consider the subject material, but "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" really dials back the gore. As an example, here are two gruesome moments depicted in the original book that aren't nearly as gross in the film adaptation of "Sunrise on the Reaping.".

In both versions of "Sunrise on the Reaping," Haymitch and his fellow District 12 tributes, including Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), align themselves not with the super-charged Career tributes from wealthy districts but other underdogs, dubbing themselves "the Newcomers." One of those Newcomers is Ampert Latier (Percy Daggs IV), the son of former District 3 victor Beetee Latier (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) who's only in the Games because the Capitol wants to punish Beetee for insubordination.

Ampert, Beetee, and Haymitch hatch a plan to smuggle an explosive into the arena and blow up a water tank that could flood the entire mechanism of the arena, and though Haymitch does set it off, the arena survives ... and the Gamemakers summarily punish him by killing Ampert with "muttations," or genetically engineered animals, in the form of squirrels. "I never even get a glimpse of Ampert, just writhing furry bodies fighting for a piece of him," Haymitch states in the book, and the movie does show this. It does not, however, show this:.

"Panting, I watch them fade away. Then I turn back to what I am meant to witness. A small white skeleton, stripped clean to the bone. No flesh or clothing remains, only an ax at its right side, my knife at its left. My lips move, but no sound comes out. 'Buddy?' I stumble forward, spotting his tracker, wedged just below his elbow. There is no one to comfort, to ease out of this world. Ampert's been swallowed up by the Capitol, and his coffin will hold only these pearly white bones.".

In the on-screen version, we simply see Ampert's body — not a clean skeleton.

Another newcomer that forms an alliance with Haymitch and Maysilee is Wellie, a diminutive District 6 tribute who's played in the film by Rada Rae. In the movie, as the tributes' numbers start to dwindle, Haymitch hears Wellie's token — a small bicycle bell — and is lured into a trap by Career tribute and formidable District 1 player Silka Sharp (Laura Marcus). The movie then skips ahead to that finale showdown between Silka and Haymitch, from which Haymitch emerges as the victor. The book is, again, far more explicit:.

In a recent development, "Rounding a final clump of saplings, I freeze in horror at what awaits. Silka stands like a statue, her snot-green outfit splattered in bright red. In her right hand, her ax. Her left holds Wellie's head, eyes still open, mouth agape. The only movement, the only sound, comes from the blood dripping into the pine needles on the forest floor. Wellie's body lies crumpled in a heap a few feet away. The shiny silver bicycle bell. The blowgun. The child-sized boots. The tiny knife in her bird claw. Dove-colored feathers. Headless baby chick. I could live ten thousand years and never erase this sight from my memory.".

It makes complete sense that the film version of "Sunrise on the Reaping" doesn't feature a kid's decapitated head — the movie is rated PG-13, after all. Still, if you haven't read "Sunrise on the Reaping," you should (it's really good!), and you should also know that it dials up the violence ante in a significant way. "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," which is overall extremely true to the book but scales back some of its most stomach-churning moments, is in theaters now.

The One Thing About GTA 6's Ending to Know Before You Get Too Far In

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that while playing through Grand Theft Auto 6, you might notice that there are a lot of systems that can alter your experience.
  • In a recent development, be warned, though: every choice you make really, really matters.
  • note: This article contains spoilers for GTA 6’s ending.].
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that while playing through Grand Theft Auto 6, you might notice that there are a lot of systems that can alter your experience. There’s the relationship system, your criminal profile, fitness routines that change your physique, and plenty more that gives you a lot of control over Jason and Lucia. In the moment-to-moment gameplay, it can be a little hard to figure out how much of that actually has an impact on the game.

In a recent development, be warned, though: every choice you make really, really matters. GTA 6 features multiple endings that will be shaped by how much you engage with its systems. And it never makes it clear that those choices matter.

[Ed. note: This article contains spoilers for GTA 6’s ending.].

In a recent development, while I won’t reveal how my playthrough ended, I will note that I was faced with a binary choice that could have pushed me toward two different endings. GTA 6 has a few branching narrative moments like this where players are presented with two choices, so that lined up with the rest of the game. In my mind, I assumed that the game only had two endings. That was very incorrect.

Recent findings suggest that that revelation came when Polygon spoke with Rockstar North co-head Rob Nelson ahead of GTA 6’s release. I had just rolled credits on the game, and Nelson was eager to learn which ending I got. I told him, and made a comment about the binary choice. He revealed that there were actually several possible endings with varying degrees of difference. Nelson said that some of them are small, maybe changing a bit of dialogue in a scene.

Industry observers note that others are more drastic. The climactic moment of my ending took place on a specific bridge on the map. Nelson stated that some endings don’t go there at all. And while I’ve yet to see every ending play out (nor do I even know how many endings there are), I’ve already gotten the sense that the fates of certain characters can even change from ending to ending. If someone tries to spoil exactly what happens in GTA 6’s ending for you, know that you might end up getting surprised when something completely different occurs in your playthrough.

So, what determines which ending you get? Nelson told me that a few different factors go into it. The most obvious one is the choices that you make during branching story moments. You can also probably guess that the relationship system plays into it too. Your criminal profile is a factor as well, so even your choice of using lethal force in various situations can make a difference. On top of that, your ending can also change based on how much money you’ve stashed into your family savings account by the time you hit the credits. Needless to say, no decision goes without consequence in GTA 6.

If you’re stressing out about getting the “bad” ending by accident, don’t worry too much. Nelson noted that there aren’t exactly good or bad endings in GTA 6. Without spoiling where my story went, I can see where he’s coming from. The ending I got made perfect sense with the way I had been playing. And even within that moment, I still had a choice as to how it could play out. So long as you’re making deliberate choices in GTA 6 and not just ignoring systems for the heck of it, you should hopefully land on an ending that matches your playstyle. But keep all this in mind if you decide to ignore Jason and Lucia’s relationship. You’ll feel that eventually.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most prominent figures of the so-called Bluenami was not a candidate on the ballot, but rather a Twitch streamer and political commentator: Hasan Piker.

According to recent reports, this year Hasan was involved in dozens of races across the country, campaigning for progressive candidates like Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed. But you’re probably more likely to associate Hasan’s name with what other people have had to say about him—from Fox News commentators to more established members of the Democratic Party.

Recent findings suggest that hasan regularly courts controversy on both his hours-long Twitch streams, where he’s mentioned things like “America deserved 9/11,” and social media, where he’s written that Hamas “is a thousand times better than” Israel. He claims he’s often taken out of context, and that his audience knows what he really means—and where he stands. In his mind, he’s a leftist provocateur, maybe, but one who understands the importance of working-class values and electoral strategy.

While Hasan has walked back some of his more inflammatory language, his rhetoric raises the question: Is he a liability to the cause he champions? Or is he successfully reaching the critical audience—namely, young men—that helped elect the wave of progressives poised to take office in January?

According to recent reports, with 2028 on the horizon, I wanted to know how Hasan thinks about his growing platform, and if he sees his role shifting in the media landscape. What responsibility does he have to his viewers and to the candidates he supports? And does he regret any of those past statements?

We also got into the DSA’s more extreme positions and how to make sense of them; why he thinks the Republicans put his thirst trap on the jumbotron at their convention; and how he, a self-proclaimed socialist, thinks about his own money.

Mark Guiducci: Hasan Piker, welcome to Fair Game.

Hasan Piker: Very excited to be here.

Thanks for coming. Hasan, you are more online than just about anyone. You spend at least seven hours a day streaming. You reach tens of thousands of people at a time on average, and it’s all in the channel that you control. I’m curious, what are you doing here with me today? Why are you showing up for a show with a legacy media publication? What’s in it for you?

It has been revealed that well, I saw the clips and everybody looked really good. The lighting was perfect. I saw the Dari[aliza Avila Chevalier] clips, I saw Ta-Nehisi [Coates], and I was like, I got to get in on that.

Yeah. So shouts out to the team. You guys did a phenomenal job lighting this up. It looks very cool too.

According to recent reports, okay. We’ll take the compliment.

But the serious answer is, I mean, I reach an audience that obviously does not watch television, does not read legacy publications at all. And I want to show people that read Vanity Fair that I am not a terrorist.

Industry observers note that right. Which brings me to my next question because—.

Yeah, exactly. That would be the name of the episode. You’ve been everywhere this year, and you became this kind of bogeyman for the right, who probably have never heard you, watched your stream, or heard anything you’ve mentioned out of your mouth. They’ve just heard quotes repeated by news anchors. And not even just for the right, even for some on the left. And you played this interesting role because you were a surrogate and a media figure and then a media figure covering the media as well. I want to spend a little bit of time talking about how you see your role. And to start, do you consider yourself a journalist?

In a recent development, okay. Because it’s like you present this interesting new type of figure. I was thinking about how you’ve done an interview with CNN, you’ve done interviews with MS NOW, but they don’t have you on as much as I would expect them to.

I have some thoughts, but I wonder why you think that is.

I think I’ve pissed off a bunch of executives over there, because, in my experience, there are plenty of amazing reporters and journalists and producers that I know that work at all of these newsrooms, right? But from what I have seen, the masthead has a very different editorial slant than sometimes what the reporters want to cover.

Because they talk about you a lot.

They talk about me a lot. And also I’ve never been invited on any of these outlets as a pundit either, which is also strange because, as you also pointed to, I don’t just operate as a campaignster. As a matter of fact, that’s something I did very briefly and I did not like it at all. I’m first and foremost a commentator…. I do have the capacity to do journalism at times. I’ll do interviews with candidates. I’ll go out and—.

Well, candidates I like. Sometimes I do interviews with candidates I don’t like or I’m unsure about as well. The problem is most of the candidates don’t want to come on if they know I’m gonna cook ’em. Like Gavin Newsom, I have had feelers out to get him on the broadcast.

I have. Gavin, Gavin, come on the show. I am a taxpaying California resident. I’m one of your constituents. You want to be president in 2028, you’re gonna have to be able to talk to people like myself.

All right. So, Hasan, this cycle you were involved in some way in, by one count, 48 different candidates’ races, and AIPAC and pro-Israel groups spent about $101 million in those races. And on Election Day, your stream was the second most watched in the country after NBC News’s “Kornacki Cam.” With a little bit of distance, how are you thinking about what happened a couple of weeks ago, both for yourself and for the country?

I feel a lot of hope. Hopefully it’s not going to be short-lived. But I feel very excited for the first time in a very long time, after 10 years of some of the most odious politics that we’ve seen from Trumpism, from MAGA. We finally saw a real sea change through electoralism. People truly have had enough with Trumpism.

I wouldn’t be so certain because I feel like if there’s one controlled opposition party that is capable of breathing life back into MAGA, it would be the establishment Democrats. So I’m a little bit worried, but it’s very clear that people are truly fed up.

All right. So there are a couple of different narratives that are coming out of the midterms right now. Rahm Emanuel, for instance, is touting this as a victory for moderate Democrats, saying that they ran 21 points above Kamala Harris. The DSA, meanwhile, is claiming that American voters have “emphatically endorsed socialism.” Other pundits are saying that these significant gains have nothing to do with the Democrats and are actually about the war in Iran and high gas prices. So does this debate between moderates and progressives feel like a healthy back-and-forth to you, or does this feel like the newly introduced aisle that has to be straddled?

In a recent development, I mean, I think this is not even a new debate. This factional battle has existed within the Democratic Party and perhaps—.

Yeah, but the progressive wing was always really fringe.

And now we’re talking about—I don’t know if 50/50 is right. I don’t want to use numbers, but—.

I think it’s a testament to our success, especially in the midterms, that there are a lot of people who are trying to protect their comfortable sinecures and are outright panicking. And all of that completely sidesteps the reality that the vulgar Bernie-ism of 2016 was echoed through every single candidacy, every single campaign all across the country, from the obvious Berniecrats like Abdul El-Sayed to even people like Roy Cooper, who in the past were very moderate, very centrist. And he still is a center-right figure, which clearly works in North Carolina. But even he was railing against data centers, billionaires, the uncertainty surrounding AI. I mean, this is left populism. And that rhetoric, one could say, was deployed in the past by even the likes of Bill Clinton and Al Gore.

But for some strange reason, there was a turning point in 2016 where the Democratic Party adopted this strange role of defending the corporate class and defending the elites and took ownership over, I guess, defending these institutions overall. And these institutions are worthy of defending, for the record. However, from the perspective of the masses, if the government is failing them, if these institutions are failing them, then they wanted someone to break it. And that was obviously the right populism of Donald Trump. And break those institutions, he surely did. And we’ve seen the devastating results of that.

So you credit the progressivism with what happened on election night?

According to recent reports, absolutely. I mean, there’s certainly local moderation on concerns, right? Because James Talarico went from saying “God is nonbinary” to “we need to defend our transgender brothers and sisters, our neighbors,” which is, again, insanely woke for Texas, or just in general, right? There are far more conservative figures in the party than James Talarico’s current position on the trans concern.

According to recent reports, okay. But sometimes the way that you run—oftentimes the way that you run needs to be different than the way that you govern or lead once you’re there. Do you think it is productive to continue pushing some of the farther-left ideas once they get to Congress? Or is pragmatism and getting things done, you know, defining things that are really achievable and sticking to them as a bloc, as a group, and pushing them over the line— when you’re talking to some of these winners, are you talking about [that]?

I think if I could speak to the entire incoming freshman class or the entire caucus—.

Recent findings suggest that I would say, be bold, be brave, and obviously immediately implement accountability. Investigations are an absolute must. This is what people are demanding. After the economy, the second concern, the biggest concern, is corruption. The second term with Trump has been unbelievable. I mean, look, I’m Turkish. I’ve seen corruption in the Turkish government. I’ve seen corruption and tracked it and talked about it all around the world with different governments. I’ve never seen anything like what the Trump administration has done because of how flagrant and in your face it was. I don’t think anyone is above the law. We have to restore law and order. So I’m a law-and-order Democrat. And I know that sounds something very different in Washington, DC, or in general. I think when politicians say that, they mean, like, punish the poor for minor crimes. I’m talking about punishing the wealthy for their corruption, for their major crimes, because they’re the ones who are robbing people blind.

But, you know, a lot of people would say that impeachment would be a distraction. So I guess what I’m saying is, if you had to choose three agenda items that the Democrats are agreeing on and they’re going forward with—you already said subpoenas and investigations.

Industry observers note that what else? What are the other two that in the first year you really want to see happen?

I think it’s virtually impossible [with] the current DOJ to—they’re not impartial, right? I don’t think that we are going to move the needle on actual criminal investigations before the Democrats win the White House in 2028. But all of this is building up for that moment. And for that reason, I think we need to talk about affordability—and not just simply talk about affordability, but also explain how we’re going to solve the affordability crisis through a comprehensive legislative agenda. And one of the major issues around affordability that is oftentimes discussed as a separate thing, but it’s not, is health care. And the Democratic Party’s approach to health care has been lackluster. Even though Americans obviously overwhelmingly trust the Democrats with fixing health care or solving the problem with health care, the reality of the matter is, while the ACA was a fantastic improvement to what existed previously, it’s not enough, and we have to move the needle in a healthier direction. We have to push for a single-payer health care solution.

Recent findings suggest that I’m perfectly fine with that. I’ve joked about that for years ’cause he’s so invested. He’s such a petty despot and so narcissistic that—.

Industry observers note that yes. I have pitched this over and over again on my show. Look, you win so big with Donald Trump if you go to Donald Trump and you say, “Look, Obamacare, not the best, right? Now you get to destroy Obamacare and you get to build something else in your name. We call it Trumpcare. It’s single-payer. It’s Medicare for All.” I think he would do it.

It has been revealed that look at this. Bipartisan collaboration.

Industry observers note that yes, I’m pragmatic. I’m bipartisan.

All right, so let’s take a step back. You were talking a second ago about how Talarico was woke. And on November 4, Twitter, formerly known as X, was amazing. Memes, jokes, you know.

I see what you did there. Yeah. We flipped it back.

Yeah, we flipped it back. With the Democrats’ victory, the idea that woke was back, do you think that’s true? Do you think that we’re going to see, culturally, the return of this idea of woke? And do you think that’s a good thing for the Democrats?

Yes. I do think that the pendulum swing was an inevitability. I talked about this quite a bit. I saw the early warning signs when [Joe] Biden won. That was one of my major warnings that young men were going to go back to the Gamergate era of very far-right politics because the Biden administration was not delivering. Recent findings suggest that definitely. The idea of woke now, though, I'm just curious—being politically correct or precise in one’s language was, for a time, an outward indication of being a progressive or maybe even being a good person in culture. Do you think that’s still the case?

I mean, I’m progressive, so I think so, but I’m a little biased. But I will say this: I think that there were certainly social excesses, which is ironic because this whole Woke 1.0, 2.0 distinction, I feel a little responsible for in the discourse because I jokingly used to say—.

Yeah, now I’ve joked about that too, and now journalists are reaching out to me being like, “Do you think Woke 3.0 is real?” I’m like, “I’m joking, guys. It’s not serious.” But here’s the thing, there is a little bit of sincerity there. I think one of the things that I routinely criticized during that 2016-to-2022, 2023, era of, I guess, Woke 1.0 was the social excesses, the maximalist demands, the inability to understand that people are complex and don’t have the same lived experience that everybody else has. Recent findings suggest that and on the other side, people will say, “Oh, that’s normalizing this kind of behavior. It’s unacceptable.” And I totally see the other side of that argument as well, but I think, especially if you’re campaigning or especially if you’re building a movement, you do have to be a little bit more understanding and not be so hardheaded and assume that everyone has to agree with you from the jump without you making a convincing case as to why you might be correct.

Recent findings suggest that okay. All right. So we’ve talked a lot about what you think about the political landscape, but I want to talk also about your role in it right now and going forward. So initially, you were called the Joe Rogan of the left. Recently, you’ve mentioned you operate more like a Charlie Kirk. Is that the right analog for the kind of influence you want to have? And if not, is there another?

I don’t think there is an appropriate analog because I’m everything all at once at the same time, because I work out and I do collaborations with people who are not expressly political, so that’s kind of like Joe Rogan. I go out and operate sometimes as a campaign surrogate, and I do rallies at college campuses and I deliver speeches, so that’s kind of like Charlie Kirk. But then usually my day-to-day commentary is what I like to jokingly refer to as a Rush Limbaugh for Zoomers. So I do all of those things at the same time, and that’s, I think, part of the reason why it’s so hard to make sense of what I do from the perspective of someone who just doesn’t understand Twitch or doesn’t understand exactly what I’m doing and has only seen negatively framed clips or clips out of context, that kind of thing. Having noted that, on the political-ideological side of things, of course I am the furthest from all of those figures. I’m just talking about the form and function of it all.

In a recent development, okay. So it seems like you’ve been recently the guy that progressives come to when they’re trying to run a primary from the left, but then when they get to the general or to office, maybe they don’t need you as much, or they have left you behind, or they distanced themselves from you. And I think about [Zohran] Mamdani in this case. I just—.

Maybe because of that Rush Limbaugh–esque heightened rhetoric; do you agree with that characterization? And how does that make you feel?

Well, my feelings are immaterial in this. As long as they’re delivering, I think that’s what matters. I’ve mentioned this before: I love Zohran and, off the rip, my attitude on this was always just put the policies in the bag. If you’re delivering for the people of Upcoming York, and if you’re delivering successfully and every success that you have as a democratic socialist mayor of New York bodes well for the rest of this movement, then I’m happy.

Yeah, but are you talking to him behind the scenes? There’s still a relationship there? Because honestly—.

In a recent development, yes. But the thing is, what I’m doing is too new for people to fully realize, to fully comprehend. So of course there’s going to be some growing pains as far as how to navigate through an unbelievably contentious media environment, especially if the candidate[s] themselves are Muslim. And, you know, I think that is the reason why—the two major figures that I can point to that have done a little bit of distancing, at least in rhetoric, even though they never disavow the platform, disavow the person, they just say, “Oh, I don’t agree with that statement”—those two figures are Abdul El-Sayed and Zohran Mamdani. They’re both very progressive. One’s a democratic socialist, the other one’s not, but they’re still very progressive for American politics, and they’re Muslim. I think that is a big part of the reason why I’ve given them a lot more bandwidth to operate in this space in whichever way they want to, because the expectation or the fears that they have are very real. As someone who has been at the center of a lot of this manufactured outrage, a lot of this controversy, being presented as an Islamist, jihadist at times, a terrorist, I know the role that the first Muslim senator has to play on the campaign trail. So you intellectually understand it, but do you feel used?

Sources indicate that I would only feel that way if they did not follow through on their promises that they made on the campaign trail. If Abdul came out tomorrow and was like, “Money out of politics? Maybe money in politics. Money in your pocket? Maybe you don’t get money in your pocket. Medicare for All? Medicare for some”—if he were to just flip the script on not just me, but Michiganders and America as a whole, then I would feel very betrayed.

According to recent reports, so we talked a little bit earlier about your audience at the very beginning. You know, you’re an interesting figure for them. There are a significant number of them that are with you for hours on end a day, and I think they probably look up to you. What responsibility do you feel to the people who watch your streams?

As far as the responsibilities that I have, I am very aware of them. I see myself as, in some respects, NPR for Zoomers. For many people, and now even an older audience as well, I am their primary news outlet. They have me on in the background, and I’m offering news and commentary throughout the day while they’re going through and doing their chores or at work with me blasting in one ear. So I know that if I were to stop randomly, people would feel it, because I see it as—I listen to The Daily; I listen to NPR every morning. If somehow I wake up one morning and NPR is no longer on, I’d be like, What happened? How am I gonna figure out what’s going on in the world?

Yeah, that’s just a lot of pressure, though, because NPR has a whole staff of people that, [if] someone’s sick, someone can pinch-hit.

According to recent reports, I mean, I’m fine living in that environment. I’m happy to do it. I’m happy to take on that responsibility.

Sources indicate that can I ask, what’s your personal life like right now? I mean, that is a lot of time on the air, and probably you have to read the news yourself too. So are you seeing friends a lot? Do you see your family a lot?

Recent findings suggest that I keep my private life private for obvious reasons ’cause there are a lot of insane people out there. But yes, I do spend a good deal of time with friends and family. I have normie friends as well that are just completely removed from the world of politics and from the world of Hollywood, influencers, that kind of thing.

Sources indicate that yeah, no, they keep me grounded, for sure, and my family certainly does as well. I spend every waking moment that I’m not on camera doing things like that, you know, enjoying the finer things in life.

Do you think of yourself as a role model?

Sources indicate that in some respects, yes. I don’t think people should follow everything that I do to a T, but I definitely do see that. I recognize the responsibility that influencers have over so many people, and I try to put my best foot forward in an effort to cultivate a nicer space on the internet, one that is more productive for people. I try to urge people to go out and unionize in their workplaces, join the Democratic Socialists of America, but then also at the same time, I try to get them to go out and work out. I’m very open about my fitness journey, my health journey. And the same even goes for my presentation. I’ve gone through these different eras now on my broadcast. Right now we’re in the suit arc. And then I sometimes see that reflected in the crowd as well when I go out to these rallies. I start seeing people also wearing suits, which is a little strange to experience, but it’s not the worst thing, right?

I think that’s a good influence.

Yeah, I think that is a good influence. You’re rocking a nice suit yourself.

According to recent reports, I bought this at a photo shoot for Days magazine. This stylist had pulled this and I loved it.

I literally was like, “I’m buying this from you.” And then since then, she’s been pulling stuff for me.

Can I ask, are you having fun? Because it seems like you are, but then what we were talking about before, with the way that you might feel abandoned—and especially the past few months, this cycle, has it been fun?

All of a sudden you’re like, Okay, well, who’s on my side now? I have nobody to push back.

Sources indicate that you’re playing this game where you try to find the worst quotes that you can and frame them as negatively as you can, and then attack candidates that might not even know the context behind some of these words. So to reduce someone to a couple of choice clips is obviously going to never give you the full picture.” I mean, he didn’t use all those words.

It’s not about being a person; it’s about being a cudgel, just something that you can use as a counterbalance.

In a recent development, I don’t think liberals, and even the left broadly, [are] ready for how to deal with that because we’ve never really had a person like me in the past. Buckley all the way to Rush Limbaugh and Charlie Kirk and numerous other far-right figures, that they know how to brush this aside. Okay. So you’re streaming most of the day, you’re reacting to news in real time, and just even by your own admission, you’ve remarked some—I think you said “silly things.” I would say some pretty extreme things along the way.

Recent findings suggest that yeah, it is, but it also isn’t because I have apologized and taken back some of the things that I’ve mentioned and apologized for how I worded or framed things. Do you feel like someone in your role has a different responsibility with their words or their public platform than an elected official or even a journalist?

It has been revealed that but what I will say is this: A lot of people don’t realize that this is an interactive medium. Most people think, when they see a clip, especially if it’s chopped a certain way—.

Yes. Most people think this is my preproduced, prescripted statement ’cause that’s all they’ve seen from the Jake Tappers of the world. They don’t realize that I am offering extemporaneous commentary on a breaking news story in real time, without a production team, while simultaneously—.

In a recent development, no. While simultaneously duking it out with anonymous accounts. What is the one thing that everybody hates on Twitter and everywhere else on the internet?

We’ve got to get you a practice.
