Arguably the greatest Christmas franchise of all time is getting its star back. 34 years after 1992's "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York," Macaulay Culkin is set to return as Kevin McCallister in a third movie that will act as a sequel/reboot for the saga.

Sources indicate that in July 2026, we got an patch on "Home Alone 3" (as we'll call it until further notice) that suggested Culkin's return was more likely than ever, as the actor reportedly paid a visit to the Disney lot where he met with studio head David Greenbaum. Now, in his What I'm Hearing newsletter over at Puck, Matthew Belloni reports that the 46-year-old actor will indeed appear in a new "Home Alone" movie.

In a recent development, according to Belloni, the "sequel/reboot" is "officially in development," with longtime writing partners Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg producing under their Point Grey banner. The report claims Rogen and Greenberg will finish up an original horror comedy project for Universal before working with Culkin on a script for the new "Home Alone" film. That's good news, as the duo couldn't be better suited to the material. (Disney, of course, has yet to officially confirm any of this.).

According to recent reports, ever since "Lost in Fresh York," the "Home Alone" franchise has delivered sequel after sequel that didn't need to happen — the most recent being the Mouse House's, to date, one and only attempt, following the Disney/Fox merger, to revitalize the saga with a sixth movie. But "Home Sweet Home Alone" once again failed to bring back Kevin McCallister. Now, however, things look set to change.

In 2025, Macaulay Culkin embarked on a "Nostalgic Night With Macaulay Culkin" tour, during which he spoke about his surprisingly great-sounding idea for a "Home Alone 3" movie. Culkin's film would follow an adult Kevin McCallister who's become too focused on work at the expense of his young son. Kevin would then become locked out of his own house with his son still inside before having to break back in and avoid his son's ingenious traps in what is essentially a metaphor for working his way back into his son's heart. Not bad, right? For now, it remains unclear whether this is, in fact, the pitch Disney has greenlit, but it would make sense.

It has been revealed that culkin has seemingly been warming up to the property over the past couple of years. As mentioned, 2025 saw him launch the "Nostalgic Night" tour, during which he chatted positively about his previous two "Home Alone" movies. Then, in 2026, he played a grown-up Kevin in a McDonald's commercial. Now, pending official confirmation from Disney, it seems he'll return to the franchise proper, with Matt Belloni noting how the actor's two young sons likely played into his decision.

In a recent development, belloni also highlighted the massive popularity of Culkin's first two films, which reliably shoot to the top of the most-watched streaming charts every holiday season. Per FlixPatrol, right on cue, the original "Home Alone" is back in the Disney+ movie charts, jumping from number seven on November 15, 2026, to number two as of the following day, where it sits at the time of writing. The other films in the saga? Nowhere to be seen. Lord knows the "Home Alone" movies need a major revitalization, and you couldn't do better than Culkin's return in that regard.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bill Hader‘s first film as a director has found its distribution partner. Black Bear has acquired North American distribution rights to “They Know,” Hader’s upcoming psychological horror film that he co-stars in with Linda Cardellini. The growing distributor, which just released “Wicker” nationwide, acquired the rights from financier MRC in what was described as a competitive situation.

Per an official synopsis, “They Know” follows a divorced dad who becomes increasingly suspicious and paranoid that his ex-wife’s latest mysterious partner is exerting a strange, unsettling influence on their children.

“Bill Hader is a singular talent both in front of and behind the camera, and he has delivered a film in ‘They Know’ unlike anything we’ve ever seen,” Black Bear president of production & operations Michael Heimler noted in a statement. “’They Know’ is authentic, original, and bold filmmaking at the highest level, and we couldn’t be more excited to partner with Bill and re-team with our great friends at MRC, who consistently deliver boundary-pushing films that help define their genre.” Related Stories Why Good Voice Acting Doesn’t Have to Happen in Isolation Watch the ‘Backrooms’ VFX Supervisor Explain His Unique Process of Collaborating with Kane Parsons.

Hader co-wrote “They Know” with Duffy Boudreau and produced alongside Bob Graf, with Alyssa Donovan co-producing.

Recent findings suggest that hader is a three-time Primetime Emmy winner for his work on “South Park” and “Barry.” He co-created the HBO comedy “Barry” with Alec Berg and began directing episodes in Season 2, gradually working his way up to directing the entirety of Season 4. He has long been open about his cinematic influences and his desire to transition into feature filmmaking after the show ended.

Hader recently shared some more details about directing his first feature while speaking at IndieWire’s Los Angeles Future of Filmmaking Summit. He explained that “They Know” emerged after he and longtime friend and writing partner Boudreau both went through divorces and discussed their biggest fears about ways the process could have gone awry.

“We’re both divorced. We were talking about how lucky we were that we were on, like, we had really good terms with our ex-wives, and we have kids with them,” Hader said. “We started talking about the worst case scenarios of, ‘Oh, my god, this person is going through this and this person is going through that.’ And then this idea came up.”.

Black Bear has yet to announce a release date for “They Know.”.

Tech Report: I Analyzed the Seven Biggest AI Chatbots to Determine How Safe They Are for Kids

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications.
  • The major AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe.
  • OpenAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications. At the same time, an increasing number of apps and services are becoming age-gated in a growing number of countries around the world, as governments realize that letting kids loose on AI apps, social media platforms, and the web at large might not be the best idea for their ongoing development and prosperity.

The major AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe. If you want to know what youngsters in your family may be getting exposed to, and what you can do about it, here's the rundown.

OpenAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls. The minimum age for customers is 13, and if you're under 18, you need to have parental consent to open an account—age is predicted via several signals, including what times of day you use ChatGPT and what you talk about.

Industry observers note that accounts for under-18s automatically become ChatGPT for Teens accounts. There's more of a focus on learning and study (with a dedicated study mode), as well as "age-appropriate safeguards to help reduce exposure to sensitive or potentially harmful content." There are built-in protections for "harmful topics," including sexual, romantic, or violent roleplay, graphic violence, and self-harm. These work on top of the safeguards for all users that limit chats about physical harm and illegal activity.

Recent findings suggest that these ChatGPT for Teens accounts can also be linked to a parental account—but while parental consent is required for under-18s to use the service, ChatGPT clearly says that teens do have the option to break the link if they want. If you do persuade your kid to keep your accounts connected, you can set time limits on when the AI bot can be used, and tweak some of the sensitivity settings. However, you can't view any conversations.

According to recent reports, to set up parental controls from ChatGPT on the web, click your profile icon (bottom left), then Settings > Parental controls > Add family member and follow the instructions. It's also worth bearing in mind that ChatGPT app can also be used for free, anonymously, in any web browser, though OpenAI states consumers accessing the AI this way are subject to the default under-18s limits (and can't save chats or access an archive).

Sources indicate that gemini is tied into everything else Google does, and follows the broader rules for Google accounts: No under-13s, unless you're part of a family group and using an account managed by an adult. You can manage your family through the Family Link portal on the web, though as far as parental controls specific to Gemini go, you can only enable or disable access to the AI (settings like screen time apply across all enabled apps).

Industry observers note that for all under-18s (partly identified through age estimation), whether or not they're part of a managed family group, Google applies some additional protections. They include preventing the AI from taking on a persona, guarding against emotional dependence on the AI, and discouraging bullying and other forms of harassment. There are also safeguards to limit chats about age-restricted substances like alcohol or vapes, and mental health issues like eating disorders.

These protections for minors are applied in addition to the usual guardrails in Gemini for everyone. The guardrails should lead you away from conversations about self-harm, suicide, violence, and illegal activities, and offer quick links to support in times of crisis. However, Google itself admits that these filters aren't perfect.

According to recent reports, as with ChatGPT, there's a loophole of sorts in that anyone can start chatting with Gemini, for free inside a web browser, with no checks at all. These conversations can't be saved and come up against usage limits fairly quickly, but they're only protected by the general restrictions for all accounts, not the ones specific to minors.

Industry observers note that meta AI will show up in several apps that young people and children are likely to use, including WhatsApp and Instagram, as well as having its own separate app on the web and on phones. The standard restrictions for Meta's social media accounts apply to its AI too: A minimum age of 13, and restrictions for all under-18s. Like many other platforms, it uses some AI magic to flag up accounts being used by minors.

If you're under 18 and on a Meta Teen account, you'll come up against blocks if you try to get Meta AI to engage in sexual or romantic roleplay, or discuss alcohol or substance misuse. Chats on topics such as eating disorders and self-harm will prompt the AI to offer guidance towards relevant support services.

Meta offers a comprehensive parental control setup for its apps, including Meta AI, but connecting a parent account isn't compulsory for teens. This is handled through the Meta Family Center portal, and parents can get reports on the general topics that kids are chatting about with AI—though they don't get the exact transcripts or prompts. Any self-harm or suicide discussion can trigger an alert to the connected parent account.

All users, under 18 or over 18, get support and crisis intervention responses when chatting about suicide and self-harm, and there are strict limits on discussing illegal and harmful acts, including drug use and cyberbullying, as well as sexual and adult content.

Apple users have to be 13 or over to have an account, which is required to access Siri AI—anyone younger needs to have an account created for them by an adult, and these accounts can only get at the basic, older Siri. Date of birth must be declared when opening an Apple account, with tighter checks rolling out in many parts of the world.

Anyone over the age of 13 can have an Apple account and use the Siri AI app, with or without a connected parent account, as it stands in most U.S. states. This means the well-being safeguards are essentially the same for teens as they are for adults: There are safeguards around self-harm, suicide, sexual and violent content, and illegal commands. It's one of the more conservative AIs when it comes to what it will talk about.

Recent findings suggest that the upcoming and improved Siri AI can be managed to some extent by the new parental controls available in iOS 27 and Apple's other software updates for 2026—Apple has clearly seen the way the wind is blowing—but this is optional for teens. It depends on whether or not you can corral your kids into a Family Sharing group.

If your teens are in your family group of consumers, then the standard Screen Time rules apply for controlling app usage limits and device access (in iOS Settings, tap your name, then Family to get at them). There are also options for disabling certain Siri AI features, such as the writing tools or the image creation capabilities.

It has been revealed that like Gemini/Google and Apple/Siri, Copilot is tied into the wider Microsoft ecosystem, and access for under-18s can be managed through it. Users must be 13 or older to hold a Microsoft or a Copilot account—and again, there's some underlying tech in place to detect anyone who might be deliberately lying about their age.

In a recent development, if you've got a teen using Copilot, you can manage their access through the standard Microsoft Family Safety portal. You're able to enable or disable Copilot access, set times during which Copilot can and can't be used, and disable certain features like image generation or voice mode. Parents can't read the Copilot chats of their kids, though.

Parental supervision is optional—a teen aged 13–17 can use Copilot without linking their account to an adult one. Microsoft says consumers identified as under 18 won't see personalized results or ads, and will get age-appropriate responses regarding risky or harmful content, though there's not much detail on what that entails.

More generally, content around self-harm, violence, adult content, harassment, and harmful or illegal activity is banned on the AI platform. Any prompts about suicide or drugs will bring up support options rather than answers, whether you're an adult or a young person using the service.

Industry observers note that ultimately that means that minors have the same access to Grok as adults, if they want it—an AI platform that combines "weak safety guardrails" and "a range of extremely harmful content" that includes "explicit sexual content, mental health risks, violent content, and inappropriate responses to... offensive content" (that's the Common Sense Media Report again).

Yes, this is the AI chatbot that has previously had a problem with deepfake porn imagery, and which has traditionally taken a rather casual attitude towards safety concerns, led by SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk. While illegal and harmful content is supposedly banned from Grok, its own FAQs admit that certain chats can result in "dialogue that may involve coarse language, crude humor, sexual situations, or violence.".

According to recent reports, there is actually a Grok Kids Mode that limits the kind of content that can be shown and the conversation topics that can be added, but it requires users to self-declare themselves as minors and is easy to bypass. The advice from Common Sense Media seems to be the way to go with Grok: Do not let your teens access it.

It has been revealed that claude's approach to child safety is straightforward: You can only register for an account if you're over 18. It is possible to lie about your age when signing up, but like the other platforms, Anthropic looks at various "signals" in behavior to spot minors—if your account gets flagged, you have to verify your age using an option like face age estimation or Yoti.

There's no free web access to the chatbot, like there is with ChatGPT and Gemini, so if you're under 18, you're locked out from the service unless you know the behavioral tricks to get past Claude's detection systems.

Recent findings suggest that in terms of more general well-being protections on Claude, any chat around self-harm or suicide will guide owners towards helplines and other resources for support. Conversations about illegal activities, disallowed speech, and explicit sexual content are banned from the platform. In recent months, Anthropic says it's also reduced AI sycophancy.

Industry observers note that that's something of a whistle-stop tour of the significant seven AI chatbots, but if you're a parent, it should give you some idea of what's out there and how easy it is to access. Besides the parental controls built into these AIs (or not), you also have the settings available at the platform level—Android, iOS, Windows, macOS—to restrict the use of any potentially harmful apps.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best-selling author of Red, White and Royal Blue has revealed their next book, and it’s far from what we’ve come to expect.

Casey McQuiston announced Friday that their long-awaited next book will be released in October 2027, and we already have the title and a synopsis. However, this next work will mark a major genre departure for the romance author with a cult following.

McQuiston, best known for clever, queer new adult and YA rom-coms like Red, White and Royal Blue, One Last Stop, and I Kissed Sara Wheeler, is officially making their foray into another beloved genre: romantasy.

According to recent reports, mcQuiston’s next novel, titled The Knight and the Bookseller, is a classic portal fantasy with a queer, romantic twist. According to the author’s brief synopsis, it follows Molly Darling, a bookseller who “stumbles out of her quiet life into the world of her beloved childhood fantasy series—and the arms of her favorite character, the heroic (and haunted) paladin Bronwyn em’Cadogan.”.

In a short video shared on Instagram Friday morning, McQuiston can be seen in medieval cosplay, wandering Latest York with a poster bearing the book’s title and release date.

The official cover is still under wraps, but McQuiston did share one more clue for fans: a list of tropes found in the novel, including “stories about stories,” “slow burn + high heat,” and “sword lesbians,” among others.

Though McQuiston has experimented with magical realist elements in past novels like One Last Stop (2021), about a woman who falls for a time-traveling subway rider, The Knight and the Bookseller will be their first full entry into the romantasy space.

Before sharing the title and synopsis on social media, McQuiston teased this genre switch-up to fans, posting a mood board to Instagram featuring images of Joan of Arc, medieval knights, and several 17th-century paintings.

Sources indicate that the clues didn’t stop there. After sharing the book’s title, McQuiston shared a set of clues about the book’s main character, Molly, including “fantasy novels,” “unused Earth Sciences degree,” “sourdough starter,” “mushroom foraging knife,” “childhood trauma,” “delayed lesbian awakening,” and “cat.”.

The clues also came with a segment of McQuiston’s character-inspired playlist, which included the songs “I Want It All” by Katie Gavin, “Ankles” by Lucy Dacus, and “Ready” by CMAT, among others.

The Knight and the Bookseller isn’t the only McQuiston release on the horizon. A companion novel to Red, White and Royal Blue, titled Red, White and Royal Blue: The Private Correspondence, releases December 1.

Described as an “epistolary novella,” The Private Correspondence is written in the form of love letters, postcards, and journal entries shared between the two main characters in Red, White and Royal Blue: first son Alex Claremont-Diaz and British Prince Henry Fox.

The novella is part companion, part sequel to the first book—the letters begin during the events of Red, White and Royal Blue and span the next 20 years of Alex and Henry’s relationship, revealing their future after the first book’s ending. Meanwhile, a sequel to the 2023 film adaptation of Red, White and Royal Blue has already wrapped filming. Titled Red, White and Royal Wedding, the sequel film is rumored to release on Prime Video before the end of the year.

The Knight and the Bookseller releases October 19, 2027. You can pre-order it here, and order Red, White and Royal Blue: The Private Correspondence, which releases December 1, here.

This article contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".

Industry observers note that "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" adapts the story that fans have been waiting for since 2008, revealing how Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), future mentor of Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence), became the victor of the 50th Hunger Games. Haymitch's games were even more brutal than usual: as a special "quarter quell" game, each of the twelve districts had to offer up four children, not two. (Haymitch ends up in the games after one of the two District 12 boys originally chosen tries to flee and then is shot.).

According to recent reports, one of the District 12 kids "reaped" alongside Haymitch is Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), the daughter of a candy shop owning family. A jewelry collector, Maysilee is the original owner of the Mockingjay pin that Katniss eventually comes to wear during the "Hunger Games" trilogy.

Now, this being a prequel where Haymitch's victory (as pyrrhic as it is) is assured, you should go into "Sunrise on the Reaping" knowing Maysilee doesn't walk out of that arena. Grace actually plays two roles in the film, the other being Maysilee's twin sister, Merrilee. Once Haymitch returns, during Maysilee's funeral, he has to see the very same face of the girl he failed.

According to recent reports, viewers, too, might recognize Maysilee and Merrilee's shared face. Mckenna Grace is a prolific young actress with many film and TV (including voiceover) roles to her name. In just the past few years, she appeared in "Five Nights at Freddy's 2" as paranormal activity hunter Lisa, Clara in the Colleen Hoover adaptation "Regretting You," and Hannah Thurman in "Scream 7." Those recent roles only scratch the surface of her acting resume.

Sources indicate that born in 2006, Mckenna Grace is a recently graduated child actress; her first acting role was on the 2012 Disney XD series "Crash and Bernstein." Soon after she had a part on soap opera "The Young and the Restless" from 2013 to 2015 as Faith Newman. Her breakout film role was in 2017 Chris Evans vehicle "Gifted," where she played young math prodigy Mary Adler.

Industry observers note that in the late 2010s, Grace found a niche playing child versions of main characters. She played young Tonya Harding in "I, Tonya," young Carol Danvers in "Captain Marvel," a young Sabrina Spellman in one episode of "The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina," and starred in Mike Flanagan's miniseries "The Haunting of Hill House" as a young version of Kate Siegel's character Theo Crain. This means she's played young versions of Margot Robbie, Brie Larson, and Kiernan Shipka. (Grace, who played Paige Swanson on sitcom "Young Sheldon," has said she envisions Reese Witherspoon as the adult version of that character.).

From 2021 to 2022, during Seasons 4 and 5 of "The Handmaid's Tale," Grace played Esther Keyes, the abused teenage wife of a much older man. This role earned her an Emmy nomination for Outstanding Guest Actress in a Drama Series. 2021 was also the year that Grace starred in "Ghostbusters: Afterlife" as Phoebe Spangler, later reprising the role in 2024's "Ghostbusters: Frozen Empire.".

One of Grace's voiceover roles was playing a young version of Daphne Blake in the 2020 animated "Scooby Doo!" film "Scoob!" Fresh off of "Sunrise on the Reaping," she's going to play Daphne again, this time in live-action, in the upcoming TV series "Scooby Doo: Origins" due out in 2027.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is playing in theaters.

#16708. Latest Update: Is A24 Finally Substantial Enough to Be Considered a Major Studio?

Latest Update: Is A24 Finally Substantial Enough to Be Considered a Major Studio?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2065 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Earlier this year when IndieWire reported that A24 had settled a dispute with Marcus Theaters over theatrical terms, a back and forth that kept some of A24‘s summer titles like “The Invite,” “Tony,” and “Onslaught” out of the fourth-largest chain in the country, the reason was because of a debate over A24’s size.
  • It has been revealed that this is the question that Hollywood — and even perhaps A24 internally — should start asking: Should A24 now be considered a major studio?
  • In some regards, this is a semantic discussion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this year when IndieWire reported that A24 had settled a dispute with Marcus Theaters over theatrical terms, a back and forth that kept some of A24‘s summer titles like “The Invite,” “Tony,” and “Onslaught” out of the fourth-largest chain in the country, the reason was because of a debate over A24’s size. When you have blockbusters as massive as “Backrooms” and “Marty Supreme,” why would you still want theatrical terms that lump you in with the specialized, little guys?

It has been revealed that this is the question that Hollywood — and even perhaps A24 internally — should start asking: Should A24 now be considered a major studio? Should A24 be in the same conversation as Disney, Universal, Sony, Paramount, Warner Bros., Netflix, Amazon MGM, Apple, and Lionsgate? Related Stories Bill Hader’s Feature Directorial Debut ‘They Know’ Lands at Black Bear Why Good Voice Acting Doesn’t Have to Happen in Isolation.

In some regards, this is a semantic discussion. Whether A24 is in that made-up tier of six to nine corporate conglomerates that the trades call “majors” doesn’t mean a lick to the general public. Audiences know they care about the A24 brand and logo in the same way they pay attention to the brands of Marvel, Pixar, Blumhouse, IMAX, and a select few others making movies today, and the rest is mostly gravy. Postrak found that on average, 70 percent of people who see A24 movies on opening weekend go to theaters more often than others, at least monthly, so the brand has an impact. But whether it has theatrical terms on par with Paramount or with Bleecker Street doesn’t matter in the slightest.

In another sense, whether A24 is a major studio and not some cool upstart indie with a lot of scale matters a whole lot. It matters to investors, it matters to people who care about the A24 brand, it matters to theater owners, and it should matter to A24 itself as it defines what it wants to be moving forward. Netflix wasn’t always considered a major, legacy studio, but their size and success got so undeniable that you had to put them in the same conversation as the other majors who drove trends, who influenced deal making for stars and creators, and who eventually had to reach the same labor terms as everyone else.

A24 might soon be in the same boat, if it isn’t already. Led by the success of “Backrooms,” the organization has entered a latest echelon in 2026, one that has allowed it to rival studios that were once much larger than A24 in every facet. Now those lines have blurred, A24’s budgets and the grosses those films are able to generate have grown, it’s earning sizable $75 million investments from places like Google and is in the mix to buy properties like Letterboxd, arguably more than others have speculated its time to sell.

In a recent development, answering whether A24 is a “major” isn’t a simple question with one answer. There’s several criteria we could look at to make a case in either direction.

A24 through November 15 in 2026 has earned $526.6 million at the domestic box office, according to data from Rentrak. It was led by “Backrooms,” which made $197 million domestic, but that’s not even half its overall haul. This year, that’s roughly $175 million above the next-highest specialized distributor in Focus Features ($351.8 million), which released the even more successful “Obsession” ($263.4 million) this year, and it’s well above the likes of other indie rivals like Neon, Fathom, GKIDS, Angel Studios, Black Bear, and Searchlight.

It has been revealed that it has also more than doubled what it brought in across a full year in 2025, a 124 percent increase so far (it still has its significant awards play “The Debut” opening in December and “Club Kid” going wider), and it’s nearly four times where it was in 2023 when A24’s total domestic box office was $136.7 million and its biggest release of the year was “Talk to Me,” which made $44.2 million domestic. Four of A24’s movies this year (“Backrooms,” “You Can See Everything,” “The Drama,” and “Primetime”) surpassed that figure.

In a recent development, it’s safe to say it puts A24 in a tier of its own above the other indies. But does it rise to the level of a major? As recently as last year, the answer was squarely no. But A24 in 2026, per Rentrak, commands a 6.0 percent market share on the year so far. That puts it fifth on the year so far, ahead of Warner Bros., Paramount, and Lionsgate (those numbers will change as some other tentpoles emerge). It would not have even cracked the top 10 last year when its market share was just 2.7 percent and was largely driven by the late-year success of “Marty Supreme.”.

Sources indicate that A24 doesn’t have and probably won’t for some time field a movie that can realistically sniff $1 billion worldwide the way many major studios manage to pump out each and every year. But receipts don’t lie, and what makes this realistically sustainable for A24 to repeat year after year is how much it has grown.

A24 is releasing in the vicinity of 16 to 18 movies annually, and that puts it easily on par with legacy studios like Disney, Sony, Warner Bros., and Paramount. Skydance, which now owns Paramount and WB, will release 30+ movies a year, but between the two studios. Universal tends to get into the 20s, but only when you combine its output with that of Focus. Netflix puts out way, way more than the whole bunch, but they’re naturally streaming movies that include low-budget genre movies and documentaries.

Some of A24’s films each year are still acquisitions out of festivals, which was the case this year with both “The Invite” (Sundance) and “Club Kid” (Cannes). But like the other majors, A24 produces and finances a large majority of its movies independently, with a handful of co-productions. Importantly, it works with upcoming filmmakers and forges relationships so that they stay in their pipeline, whether they’re newcomers like Lance Oppenheim and Kane Parsons or veterans like Celine Song, Alex Garland, and Ari Aster who have returned to A24 time and again.

In a recent development, A24’s international distribution has it partnering with other overseas distributors, which is structurally different from major studios that have robust international distribution arms, but it has still released some of its movies in English-language territories like the UK. You can imagine that as A24 continues to grow, that could be one area of natural expansion.

Where A24 still lags significantly behind other majors though is in its overall content spend, a number that A24 doesn’t publicly disclose. Netflix had a content spend this year of about $20 billion. Disney was around $24 billion and recently projected to increase to $26 billion in its next fiscal year. Maybe if A24 starts picking up sports rights to the NBA it can start getting into that ballpark.

But even when focusing just on film, something like “Backrooms” was still produced for a modest $10 million, whereas other studios have multiple titles that well exceed $100 million in production budget alone. We do know though that its budgets have increased dramatically as A24 pursues more tentpole properties. “Marty Supreme” was previously its most expensive title, but its adaptation of the video game “Elden Ring” will blow that out of the water, with a budget in the vicinity of $170 million or above. That kind of investment carries risks. There are Marvel movies that don’t cost that much.

It has been revealed that A24 hasn’t yet put its stamp on a four-quadrant, animated Dr. Seuss movie or something similar that would easily make you think it has ambitions of becoming a major studio, but the types of movies it has released has grown more varied over the years. It has horror movies, adult comedies, biopics, thrillers, and even, of course, documentaries like “You Can See Everything,” an area that it looked like A24 was scaling back on not too long ago. When “Elden Ring” opens it will squarely be an action fantasy, and the studio has other genre films, comedies, thrillers, and more in the works for next year.

You can also see A24’s diversity in how it’s approaching awards plays versus commercial titles or specialized fare. Something like “The Drama” this year opened wide right out of the gate given its star power, whereas others like “The Invite” and “Tony” have stuck to platform releases before going wider. And those smaller, art house titles alongside its genre movies and its tentpoles are still a key part of its business model and identity. Movies like “Pillion,” “Mother Mary,” and “The Moment” have done business on a much smaller scale, but are still key in helping the manufacturer get to that 6 percent share (they lost money on some, though).

Sources indicate that the definition of major studio today has evolved to the point that the movie division is just a component of a massive media conglomerate, one that also includes television, streaming, gaming, sports, news, theme parks, and other ancillary businesses. If you’re Apple or Amazon, your movie studio is a small cog, practically a loss leader, in the larger tech empire. It gives these companies valuations of tens of billions of dollars, and it’s why A24 could still be a target for M&A if it chooses to sell.

A24 does have its own record label for music and original movie score releases and vinyl pressing, it has been producing a podcast since 2018, it owns the Cherry Lane Theater in Fresh York for stage productions and concerts, it sells plenty of kooky merchandise, and it even has a membership program and campus ambassador program that have seen growth in recent years. They’re all things that suggest the company has more on its mind than movies.

According to recent reports, and as we wrote earlier this week, its TV unit has quietly had as strong a year as its film team. A24 has spread series across virtually every major streaming service, all of them again varying in genre, pedigree, and budget. It’s not just the number of indicates that has expanded but the executive team to support them.

It may be a strength that A24 doesn’t have its own SVOD service to support all these highlights and movies, or a broadcast network or cable channel that could further complicate things. Those businesses are very costly to operate and some are in the decline phase of their trajectories. Yet, it inherently keeps A24 in a lower tier compared to other major studios that do have their own distribution apparatus for television and can license content from other studios like A24. While Gen Z might get excited about the idea of an A24 streaming service, that’s an area of growth that’s less likely to occur in the short term. Well, unless A24 wants to raise a lot more capital.

According to recent reports, this is the qualitative assessment of whether A24 should be considered a “major” studio, the one that doesn’t lean on numbers and instead just goes on feel. A24 might argue that it is one of one, that it doesn’t belong to the world of major studios, and that the baggage that comes with that status isn’t worth it. But its leaders probably believe A24 is a step above the other indies that are almost solely distributors. Do we really think the same manufacturer that is taking a chance on movies as weird as “You Can See Everything” or “Primetime” is equivalent to a studio that might make the odd “Digger,” but is mostly interested in producing “A Minecraft Movie” and “Superman?” Is it fair to lump in A24 with Focus, Searchlight, and Sony Pictures Classics, which are quite literally just specialized labels within larger studios?

In a recent development, all that could be true, but it doesn’t mean we shouldn’t reassess how we view A24 as a organization or how we handicap its hits and misses in the same way we would with Disney or Netflix. Even if we’re not ready to call A24 a “major,” there’s certainly a major shift in where A24 sits in this industry. With great success comes an even greater spotlight.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Update, 8:41 p.m.: The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed it has ended the ground stop.

On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for all airports in the United States. If you're planning to fly this afternoon or evening, or you have friends or family doing the same, you're likely concerned about tracking flight statuses. While there's still a lot we don't know, there are tools to help track flights at this time:.

There are a number of options for tracking flights, whether you have your flight number or not. If you have the flight number, the fastest method is to Google it: Google will display a live tracker of your flight at the top of the results page. You can also head to the airline's official website to track your flight: United Airlines, for example, has a flight tracker where you can either enter your route information or your flight number. Most, if not all, airlines will have a similar tool you can use.

Alternatively, you can use a site or service that tracks all flights. FlightAware is one such site and has a flight tracker that lets you search flights—so long as you know the origin and the destination. If you have the flight number, your iPhone can help: You can enter your flight number into Spotlight search to see a live tracker, or you can text a contact your flight number, then tap the link that appears under the number to see a tracker of the flight.

According to recent reports, at this time, the exact reason isn't totally clear. According to the agency, “The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” but the FAA hasn't noted what caused those communications issues or when they expect to lift the grounding. The grounding order comes one day after a massive Microsoft outage that disrupted service for owners of Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft products. It also comes one day after Ars Technica reported that the FAA was rolling out an AI-powered tool to help manage air traffic across the country.

Sources indicate that this is only the third time in U.S. history that the FAA has made such an order—once after 9/11, and again in January of 2023 due to a pilot alert system issue; the latter ground stop lasted around 90 minutes.

Sources indicate that A smoke break at the Signature Theatre ultimately resulted in one of Lois Smith‘s most fascinating performances. The Tony Award winner met Zane Pais while they were both grabbing a quick cigarette while rehearsing plays. Pais had been an admirer of Smith’s work in stage productions like “The Inheritance” and films such as “Marjorie Prime” and “Five Easy Pieces,” and longed to collaborate.

Recent findings suggest that “She has the most amazing delivery of lines; she’s always able to do something so unexpected with the language,” Pais stated during a recent Zoom interview with Smith. “I’ve seen Lois my whole life in so many amazing highlights, just be so unbelievably present on stage and be such a generous actor, and just give these heartfelt and unexpected performances. According to recent reports, so Pais wrote a short film, “Lightning Bug,” with Smith in mind. In it, she plays Lydia, a fiercely independent nonagenarian who is being pressured into selling the family home by her son and granddaughter. But things take an unexpected turn when a strange young man crashes their dinner, giving Lydia a chance to demonstrate she hasn’t missed a step despite her advanced age.

“It was all there in the script,” Smith, who recently turned 96, said. “It wasn’t complex for me to pull it off even though the script is complex.”.

The role did require Smith to perform some fight choreography, but she seemed more nervous about singing a song on screen.

According to recent reports, “I really worried: Am I going to be able to do this?” Smith remarked. “They made me a tape, and I listened to it and listened to it and practiced. I was nervous, but it went all right.”.

“Lightning Bug” filmed over a weekend in the upstate Fresh York home of one of Pais’s relatives. It was true no-frills, all-hands effort. The cast and crew bunked in an Airbnb, and a friend of Pais’s cooked meals for everyone.

Industry observers note that “It felt like we were part of a theater troupe,” Pais said. “We’d work hard. Then in the evenings, we would have red wine and smoke cigarettes.”.

In a recent development, “I seldom smoke,” Smith interjected. “Occasionally, I’ll smoke other people’s cigarettes.”.

By morning, an orderly is dead, and Blake walks out of the prison as someone else, eager to find the scientist who experimented on him. Unfortunately, Reyes’ small act of kindness marks him, and he’ll have to find the man with many faces to stop him.

#16703. Latest Update: If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it

Latest Update: If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (781 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whatever skill you’re learning, it won’t take long before someone with experience in that particular field tells you to get your hands dirty.
  • When it comes to software engineering, we somehow lost our way, thinking that our skills won’t stop improving if we stop practicing.
  • Mind you, my point in this post is not to discuss the short term quality of code output (or recorded guitar playing, to continue the proverbial thread), but rather the skill of the craftsman practicing his craft vs the one who doesn’t practice at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whatever skill you’re learning, it won’t take long before someone with experience in that particular field tells you to get your hands dirty. It’s fine to read “Born to Run”, but you won’t be running an ultra marathon any time soon if you don’t start running. Whether it’s muscle memory, technique, physical fitness or problem solving you need to work on to reach your goals, you need to practice. This isn’t a controversial statement in any field at all, and has never really been.

Except in software engineering, somehow.

When it comes to software engineering, we somehow lost our way, thinking that our skills won’t stop improving if we stop practicing. Making such a claim in any other field would be sneered at at best. Imagine John Scofield1 saying he stopped practicing his guitar because “he was at a good enough level, musically, to maintain (and even improve!) his expertise” simply by 1) instructing others on how to play (either in vibe general terms, or with a strict spec musical notation), and then 2) listening to what they played and iterating until it sounded good enough for his next record. “My music is better”, he would claim, and moreover “actually playing the guitar was never the point anyway, there’s more to making music.”.

Mind you, my point in this post is not to discuss the short term quality of code output (or recorded guitar playing, to continue the proverbial thread), but rather the skill of the craftsman practicing his craft vs the one who doesn’t practice at all.

To make another comparison that’s arguably closer to software engineering, or at least the “writing and reasoning about code” part of it, let’s look at authors in other fields. I have no doubt that reading great prose has the potential to nudge a writer towards better writing of his/her own; in fact it’s super crucial to have creative references to draw upon - no doubt at all. But, imagine an author who 1) stopped writing, and only pursued reading and giving feedback to other writers, and worse yet 2) mostly read AI generated prose!? To be perfectly honest, I would expect a quite steady (if not exponential) decline of this author’s writing skills.

In a recent development, sure. But if we can at least agree that the code that runs our software is a non-trivial part of it (though, granted, not all of it by far: The other parts of developing and maintaining software speak even louder against using generative AI as a significant tool service!), we should aspire to be proficient in understanding how code works, what good code looks like, what to watch out for and how software architecture plays a vital part in making code Easy To Change.

Industry observers note that simply “reviewing all the code Claude produced” won’t quite cut it. And who are you trying to fool, after all; at this point you’re not really reading half of it, are you?

So I propose something that used to be a no-brainer: Keep practicing!

Which brings me to my next point:.

Industry observers note that if || while you can argue that the need for being hands-on on your software’s code varies, I propose you can’t argue that we’re still solving problems. And the moment you stop practicing solving problems is the moment you stop getting better at it, just like everything else. Simple as that. This is hardly newly introduced, btw: you could always tell who beat Doom using cheat codes and who finished the game the real way! If the end goal is to “beat the game”, then by all means cheat; if the end goal is getting good at it, then I’d advice you not to. Some lessons are only learned the hard way (trial and error), and very few are learned without effort at all. Repeated LLM usage for problem solving pounds the following premise into our brain’s wiring: If something is hard, tricky or requires effort, you shouldn’t even try. And right there goes our learning, craft and joy, right out the window.

It has been revealed that in a world where people are using AI to summarise books instead of reading them and turning to AI for therapy, I don’t want to keep using it. It feels like such a slippery slope. As literacy and numeracy rates decline, I can’t help but question whether encouraging us to rely on AI so heavily is a good idea.

It makes me wonder: are we still thinking for ourselves at all?

Please, John Scofield, don’t stop playing your guitar!

I’m not sure who Em is, but their blog is great! ↩︎.

  • Industry observers note that “ Walter, right off the bat, changed the art of screenwriting,” Karaszewski said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1972, Walter Hill was a young screenwriter with just one produced movie (“Hickey & Boggs”) behind him when he scored an enviable gig: adapting Jim Thompson’s tough-as-nails crime novel “The Getaway” for actor/producer Steve McQueen (then one of the biggest movie stars in the world) and director Sam Peckinpah (then, as now, one of the greatest directors who ever lived). On Wednesday night, Hill spoke before a packed screening at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and looked back on the movie that jump-started not only his screenwriting endeavors, but a directing career that would ultimately include classics like “The Warriors,” “48hrs.,” and “Streets of Fire.” Related Stories Short Film ‘Lightning Bug’ Gives Stage and Screen Legend Lois Smith One of Her Greatest Roles — Watch It Here Is A24 Finally Big Enough to Be Considered a Major Studio?

“The Getaway” screened as part of the museum’s “Branch Selects” series, in which the Academy’s various branches program films they feel exemplify their crafts. “The Getaway” was, appropriately enough, selected by the writers branch, and screenwriter and Academy Governor Larry Karaszewski was on hand to introduce the movie and moderate the pre-screening discussion with Hill. Karaszewski, a longtime “Getaway” enthusiast who carried newspaper ads from the movie around in his wallet when he was 10 years old, pointed out that Hill changed the entire architecture of screenwriting when he burst onto the scene in the early 1970s.

Industry observers note that “ Walter, right off the bat, changed the art of screenwriting,” Karaszewski said. “We have an award show here at the Oscars called the Sci-Tech Awards, where they give awards to things that silently change the industry and advance them into the future. I really feel that Walter Hill did that in screenwriting, but it wasn’t a technical advancement. It was a literary advancement. He changed what a page should look like as a screenplay and what it could feel like to read it.” Karaszewski went on to illustrate his point by projecting pages from Robert Bolt’s “Doctor Zhivago” screenplay and Walter Hill’s “Hard Times” side by side on the screen.

According to recent reports, “You don’t even have to read [Bolt’s script], just look at it,” Karaszewski said, pointing out the dense blocks of words compared to Hill’s lean, spare page. “You’re looking at monoliths. It’s dense, and there are camera moves and references to things you would never see on screen. Walter Hill taught screenwriters that you can strip all that away. You can still direct on the page, but not by calling for specific camera movements — just by saying what you’re seeing. Walter’s scripts are made out of short sentences and white space. He looked at the placement of each line as part of the storytelling. He turned the carriage return into an art form.”.

As Karaszewski welcomed Hill to the stage, he pointed out that “The Getaway” — a smart, terse tale of a couple (Steve McQueen and Ali MacGraw) on the run after their involvement in a botched bank robbery — represented the emergence of Hill’s developing voice. “You’ll already see the beginnings of that remarkable style, the economy, the precision, the sense that every line is pushing you toward the next image.” Yet, as Hill revealed in his lively conversation with Karaszewski, the ruthless efficiency of the pacing and the concentrated emotional impact of “The Getaway” were not easily arrived at.

In a recent development, “I think it’s much harder to adapt than it is to write an original, which is the reverse of the normal theory,” Hill said. “With an original, it’s just you at your desk with the typewriter or pen. When you’re adapting, that almost always means that somebody else owns it, so you’re not simply writing based on your own opinions about what should be in and what should be out, but there’s the producer’s opinion, and the studio’s, and the actor’s. There were all these political currents that one had to navigate.”.

In a recent development, one such political current came from megastar McQueen, who didn’t interfere much with Hill’s writing but did have one caveat that amused the screenwriter. “He wanted to play a reasonably sympathetic outlaw,” Hill said. “That was not in the Thompson sensibility. So we already had a disparity, but the producer wanted to keep Steve happy.”.

“The Getaway” began as an assignment not for Peckinpah, but for Peter Bogdanovich, who was white-hot coming off of successes like “The Last Picture Show” and “What’s Up, Doc?” Bogdanovich didn’t last long, however, given his clashes with McQueen and McQueen’s power as the film‘s star. “I couldn’t imagine two more diverse sensibilities than Steve and Peter,” Hill said, noting that he had his own disagreements with Bogdanovich over the movie’s tone but wasn’t in a position to argue. “You’ve got to remember, I was nobody. I had one screen credit. And these were significant players.”.

Industry observers note that the big players included not only Bogdanovich and McQueen, but MacGraw, hot off of the smash hit “Love Story.” MacGraw was pushed into the movie by her husband, Paramount studio chief Robert Evans, which Hill found amusing given the way everything played out. “I’m going to tread lightly here,” Hill mentioned of the behind-the-scenes melodrama involving MacGraw leaving Evans when she fell in love with McQueen. “When the material was optioned and I was hired, Bob saw the movie as a fabulous idea for Steve and Ali. It didn’t work out so well for him.”.

After Bogdanovich and McQueen butted heads, Bogdanovich was let go and Peckinpah, who McQueen had enjoyed working with on “Junior Bonner,” came in to take his place. “We were very lucky to get such a talented guy, obviously,” Hill mentioned. “I thought of him then and I think of him now as one of the great directors with a very unique sensibility. I was very privileged to work with him — which doesn’t mean he and I agreed about everything.”.

Hill’s biggest disagreement with Peckinpah had to do with a scene in which MacGraw’s character considered killing McQueen before turning the gun on his nemesis — and the man with whom MacGraw had gone to bed to secure McQueen’s early release from prison. This was a scene carried over from the book, which was darker and more paranoid than what made it to the screen given McQueen’s mandate that he be sympathetic. Hill felt that the moment no longer worked now that the relationship between McQueen and MacGraw was softer and more relatable in the novel.

“I thought that for the movie we were trying to make, you might forgive your wife for sleeping with a bad man to do a very good thing for you,” Hill remarked. “That seemed to be to be conceivable. But if your wife fell into cahoots with the bad guy and actually was thinking about killing you and actually turned the gun on you before she decided to shoot the other guy…this did not track for me. But this is the screenwriter’s dilemma: you either talk the director into your point of view, or you make the change that he wants — or somebody else will. Those are your choices.”.

Industry observers note that hill lost the argument but liked the movie Peckinpah made in the end. “He staged it beautifully,” Hill noted. “He shot it beautifully. It’s got one of Steve’s best performances. And the movie turned out to be his greatest hit. He used to call me every once in a while after I became a director and say, ‘Write me another one.'” Ironically, it was the success of “The Getaway” that put Hill in a position where didn’t have to write for other directors anymore.

According to recent reports, “Larry Gordon had a producing deal to make low-budget movies at Columbia,” Hill stated. “He would give young writers a chance to direct, because he said, ‘Even if they’re no good as directors, at least we’ll get a good script. Most of the directors I’m working with aren’t any good anyway.'” Gordon gave Hill the opportunity to direct “Hard Times,” and the rest was history. Aside from kicking off Hill’s directing career, the collaboration became the first of many between the two men. “He’s a wonderful guy and a wonderful producer.”.

According to recent reports, now in his 80s, Hill continues to write and direct (his last film was the exquisite character-driven Western “Dead for a Dollar“), plying his trade in the world of graphic novels in between film projects. “I’ve had four of them published in France,” Hill noted, joking that the only one published in America was “the least good of them,” but promising another one on the way. “You’ve got to keep your hand in somehow.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This fixes "Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock()" (CVE-2026-121481) by returning -1 for invalid inputs to EVP_EncodeBlock(): NULL input or output buffers, negative lengths, and lengths for which the encoded size does not fit in an int.
  • Returning -1 for invalid inputs is the most straightforward fix, and matches what happens in wolfSSL's compatibility layer for OpenSSL's EVP_EncodeBlock().
  • Sources indicate that I'm suggesting a similar guard for EVP_DecodeBlock().
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This fixes "Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock()" (CVE-2026-121481) by returning -1 for invalid inputs to EVP_EncodeBlock(): NULL input or output buffers, negative lengths, and lengths for which the encoded size does not fit in an int. The OpenSSL SRT has asked for it to be fixed publicly; the advisory is still pending.

Returning -1 for invalid inputs is the most straightforward fix, and matches what happens in wolfSSL's compatibility layer for OpenSSL's EVP_EncodeBlock().

Sources indicate that I'm suggesting a similar guard for EVP_DecodeBlock(). No length limit is needed here because the decoded length always fits in an int, but it is a good idea to reject NULL buffers and negative lengths.

Moreover, I propose to fix the incorrect length check in the base64encode() function of http_client.c, which rejected only len > INT_MAX.

I am adding tests in test/base64_dec_avx2_test.c to cover the upcoming behavior, and documenting the -1 returns in doc/man3/EVP_EncodeInit.pod.

Exploiting this vulnerability from the command line is possible by passing a large -proxy_pass to openssl s_client. I confirmed that GOST accepts these large passwords out of the box. However, the password has to be supplied through an environment variable (env:VAR), otherwise the command line will be too long.

Note: the pattern of CVE-2026-121481 is similar to that of CVE-2021-23840.

I'm okay making any changes that you suggest, but are you really sure about this?

Both EVP_EncodeBlock() and EVP_DecodeBlock() can legitimately return 0, so 0 is not an error for either function. EVP_EncodeBlock() returns 0 when dlen == 0, and EVP_DecodeBlock() returns 0 when the input is empty after trimming.

Also, for EVP_DecodeBlock(), the current failure paths (e.g., trimmed length not a multiple of invalid base64 characters) all return -1. So, I wanted to make sure that both EVP_EncodeBlock() and EVP_DecodeBlock() consistently return -1 on any error. As I mentioned before, returning -1 is also what WolfSSL does in its OpenSSL compatibility layer.

According to recent reports, I understand the concern that third-party callers may cast the return to size_t without checking. But are we not making things more difficult for third-party calls if both 0 and -1 can indicate errors, or if the existing EVP_DecodeBlock() errors will be changed from -1 to 0?

PS: I'm happy to make a separate commit for the problematic call site checks that Norbert pointed out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Home Alone is making a comeback at the perfect time.

The Home Alone franchise began in 1990 with John Hughes and Chris Columbus at the helm to bring the story of an eight-year-old Kevin McCallister to life. Kevin defends his home from burglars after his family forgets to bring him along on a Christmas vacation. The original movie led to six movies across theaters, television, and now streaming. The 1990 installment and its sequel continue to dominate the charts around December, and the love for the franchise is seemingly never-ending.

Industry observers note that macaulay Culkin is set to return as Kevin McCallister in a new Home Alone reboot, with Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg developing the project for Disney. Puck News reported the latest development after Culkin appeared in a McDonald's holiday ad promoting a limited-time Home Alone meal and reprising his character. Culkin hasn't portrayed the character since the 1992 sequel Home Alone 2: Lost in New York, but it appears that the actor wants to bring even more Christmas joy.

In a recent development, rogen and Goldberg are producing under the Point Grey banner, and they reportedly just closed the deal to work alongside Culkin to produce a script. Disney has yet to comment on the recent reports. It was previously reported that Culkin was interested in returning around July 2026, as the actor reportedly organized a meeting with Disney's studio head, David Greenbaum. It appears that Culkin's visit has led to Disney wanting its most beloved holiday movie to return.

Four Home Alone movies were released after Culkin's final movie in 1992, with director Chris Columbus also exiting the franchise alongside the actor. Home Alone 3, Home Alone 4: Taking Back the House, Home Alone: The Holiday Heist, and Home Sweet Home Alone all failed to launch and were complete flops with critics who felt that they did not feel as charming and lacked the magic that was certainly felt in the first two movies.

Culkin previously returned to screens as McCallister for another advertising role in 2018 to promote Google Assistant. The actor has always had a deep appreciation for his character. However, after the tragic passing of Catherine O'Hara, his on-screen mother in the Home Alone movies, the actor has expressed much regret over their "unfinished business" to appear together on-screen again and often referred to O'Hara as his "mama" in touching tributes after her death.

O'Hara's character, Kate McCallister, is the matriarch of the McCallister family and was responsible for some of the most iconic moments in arguably the biggest and most-beloved holiday movies in history. With both Rogen and Culkin at the helm, a tribute to the beloved and iconic actress, as well as John Heard, who portrayed Kevin's father, Peter, and sadly died in 2017, will certainly be shown in the long-awaited Home Alone reboot.

At the time of writing, it's unclear when Culkin will officially return to theaters in Disney's Home Alone reboot.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that in GTA 6, if you want to change time, the best option is to simply go to bed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that being able to change time in Grand Theft Auto 6 is quite helpful, as you can only start some missions at a certain time of day. Progressing through the campaign is not the only reason to do so. Some businesses are open only for a period of the day, like the bank, for example.

To help you blueprint your day, we've put this guide together explaining how to change time in GTA 6, as well as how long a day lasts.

Sources indicate that in GTA 6, if you want to change time, the best option is to simply go to bed. At Jason's house, when you approach the bed, you can interact with it and choose the "Sleep" option. Ironically, this won't make the characters fall asleep immediately.

After lying down on the bed, you can either choose to check your phone, sleep and get up. Select the "Sleep" option, and you will be able to decide when the character is waking up by setting an alarm. You can set a specific time, or you can select one of the following options: morning, night, evening, or noon. For reference, when you wake up in the morning, it means you will start a fresh day at around 7 a.m.

If you're too far from Jason's house to sleep, your next best option is to simply keep playing. Time passes naturally in GTA 6. By simply exploring the map and visiting locations, the time of the day will eventually change.

In-game days might seem like they pass too quickly as you play through the campaign, but, in general, 24 in-game hours take approximately 2 hours and 24 minutes in real life. This duration only applies outside missions, like when you're freely exploring the game and doing side activities. Whenever you start a mission, time follows the script. For example, I headed to the Rusty Anchor bar to begin the "Day Release" mission at 8 a.m., but since this mission's story takes place later in the day, the clock jumped to 3 p.m. when the mission actually started.

Industry observers note that although there's no official information on how long an in-game day lasts, we ran some tests to verify that. If you check the time by looking at your phone, pressing down on the D-pad, or even looking at the clock on the wall of Jason's kitchen, you can time the duration of a minute and discover that one in-game minute is equivalent to around six seconds in real life.

Sources indicate that multiplying six seconds by the number of minutes in 24 hours (1,440 minutes) gives us 8,640 seconds. Divide this value by 60 to find out minutes, and you'll get the final result. How time passes varies depending on the context too, which can affect the overall duration of an in-game day. When in bed in Jason's house and checking the phone, time won't pass. The same happens in certain segments of missions.

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • [Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 23, 2026 during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.
  • At this point, filmmaker Beth de Araújo is two for two.
  • Recent findings suggest that more concisely: with her “Soft & Quiet” and “Josephine,” de Araújo remains undefeated when it comes to making stunning films that I will both heartily recommend and never, ever watch again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 23, 2026 during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Sumerian Pictures will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20, with a wide release to follow on Friday, December 4.].

At this point, filmmaker Beth de Araújo is two for two. Not just in terms of the quality of her films — impeccably crafted fever dreams of very different stripes and horrifyingly similar themes — but in how these films make the viewer feel.

Recent findings suggest that more concisely: with her “Soft & Quiet” and “Josephine,” de Araújo remains undefeated when it comes to making stunning films that I will both heartily recommend and never, ever watch again. Related Stories Walter Hill on Sam Peckinpah, Steve McQueen, and His Revolutionary Screenplay for ‘The Getaway’ Short Film ‘Lightning Bug’ Gives Stage and Screen Legend Lois Smith One of Her Greatest Roles — Watch It Here.

The word that comes to mind when watching a de Araújo feature is heartsick. That applies to the feeling bestowed on both the audience and her characters (the good guys and the bad guys). While her first film, the unrelenting “Soft & Quiet,” was cleverly designed to appear as if it was shot in a single real-time take, her sophomore feature is more about the steady accumulation of dread. The heroines of “Soft & Quiet” recognize what they are dealing with almost immediately (the force of the evil that is bent on destroying them is what’s surprises most), but the star at the center of “Josephine” is not just wounded by the sickness that suddenly infiltrates her young life, but her complete lack of understanding about what is happening to her and why.

In both films, it’s not just bad deeds that upends everyday lives, it’s real evil, actual monsters, perversions that don’t only show up in a movie screen. That’s true terror.

Based loosely on an experience de Araújo, who both wrote and directed the film, experienced as a child, “Josephine” initially lulls us into a false sense of safety. It’s early morning in San Francisco, and fledgling soccer star Josephine (Mason Reeves, riveting in her first role) is getting ready for a run with her devoted dad Damien (Channing Tatum, bringing incredible girl-dad energy to the role). It’s something the pair do every Sunday morning: get up early to watch Premier League football, run through a woodsy neighboring park, and kick the ball around.

Sources indicate that for her second film, de Araújo leans less on clever camera tricks, though she and cinematographer Greta Zozula occasionally put us in Josephine’s own perspective, shooting as if we are looking through the eight-year-old’s eyes. As with “Soft & Quiet,” the gimmick works, grounding us in Josephine’s world and immersing us, if briefly, in what the world looks like from her vantage. Jo-Jo, as her dad calls her, is plucky and fun and filled with energy, so when she briefly zips ahead of her dad while on their run through Golden Gate Park, it just seems like everyday high-jinks.

But when the path forks (about as heavy-handed a metaphor as de Araújo will ever employ), Josephine goes to the left, while Damien goes to the right. What she finds there will forever alter the course of her life, and set “Josephine” off on a heart-wrenching journey with no easy answers. Curious and watchful, Josephine ducks behind a tree when she sees a woman (Syra McCarthy) running into a public bathroom at the bottom of a scrubby hill, and she sinks even further down when a young man (a bone-chilling Philip Ettinger) follows the unknown woman into the tiny building.

De Araújo’s approach to portraying on-screen violence only furthers that heartsick feeling: straightforward, unsparing, and absolutely devoid of any possibility of being compared to “torture porn.” What we see, what Josephine sees, is something no person should ever witness or experience. And that’s the root of the film’s power: how do we talk about things that we should not have words for?

When Damien arrives on the scene, it kicks off what will become one of Tatum’s best performances yet, a deep-feeling and heartbreaking exploration of layers of emotional unease. Damien does everything “right,” ensuring both Josephine and the woman are safe, chasing after the assailant, calling the cops, a neat little checklist of “how to handle an emergency.” And yet, the damage has already been done. There will be more to come.

Even when Josephine begins to seek out answers to what she’s seen (snatching her mom’s phone to search “raip,” reeling at what she discovers), it’s impossible to make sense of everything. There are things to fear she never even know existed, and the deep-seated powerlessness that overtakes her causes her to act out in chilling and increasingly volatile ways. Her parents’ reactions don’t help: her exceedingly calm mother Claire (Gemma Chan, thrilling as a character just barely holding it together) wants her to see a therapist now, her more action-oriented dad is eager to put her into self-defense classes. The mixed messages both give off (to say nothing of their own barely concealed terror) do little to help Josephine, who soon becomes someone almost entirely different than the care-free kid she just was.

Industry observers note that she also picks up a upcoming friend: Ettinger begins to appear to her, a literal haunting figure, never saying a word, yet barging into nearly every moment of Josephine’s already upended life. It’s the sort of choice another filmmaker fight fill tricksy or silly, but that de Araújo delivers with the maximum of impact. And that we, like Josephine and only Josephine, can see him only furthers our immersion into her world. It almost goes beyond empathy.

Josephine’s steadily unfolding breakdown is only compounded by the arrival of yet another situation no eight-year-old should ever have to encounter: handling the messy investigation of the crime itself. How she might help (or not) drives one more wedge between Josephine and her parents, who all have a different take on what the “right” thing to do is.

Sources indicate that if these questions sound heady and heavy, they are, but de Araújo’s masterful ability to interrogate tension on every level keeps the film clipping along, each turn both a surprise and an inevitability. The monsters are here, they are real, and they’re coming.

“Josephine” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

According to recent reports, ““The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” earned $21 million in Thursday previews and early screenings on Wednesday and is expected to dominate the box office this weekend. Analysts believe it will earn north of $100 million. The preview figures are the second-best of 2026, behind “Spider-Man: Brand Fresh Day’s” massive $72 million haul. It’s also the second-best for the “Hunger Games” franchise, just behind the $25.5 million that “Catching Fire” earned in 2013. In a recent development, “Sunrise on the Reaping” is based on Suzanne Collins’ bestselling novel of the same name. It tells the origin story of Haymitch Abernathy, the alcoholic former Hunger Games victor played by Woody Harrelson in the films. The sequel checks in with him at 16 as he’s forced to compete in gladiatorial combat. “East of Eden” breakout Joseph Zada plays Haymitch. He’s surrounded by an all-star cast that includes Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace, and Maya Hawke. Francis Lawrence, who helmed most of the series’ films, returns as director. Lionsgate, which is having a strong year at the box office thanks to “Michael,” is backing the “Hunger Games” sequel as it has the previous films.

The biggest competition for “Sunrise on the Reaping” this weekend isn’t another major movie, but the release of “Grand Theft Auto 6,” which is expected to be a phenomenon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews newly introduced releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

It has been revealed that adam and Eve have taken the blame for what happened in the Garden of Eden for thousands of years, and Matthew Medney would like a word with the gods who built it. In his version of paradise, violence is already a fact of life by the time anyone has the vocabulary to call it a sin. The people who put humanity there still haven’t settled how much of a say humans should get in what happens to them. That’s quite a mess for two people to inherit before either of them gets anywhere near the fruit.

Medney, the former publisher of Heavy Metal, was more interested in what Adam and Eve took with them when they left. Once you know you’re going to die, there’s a reason to finish something while you’re here, and maybe even leave something behind for the person who comes next. It’s a strange upside to getting thrown out of paradise, and it sent Medney to a writer who’d already spent some time in the garden himself.

Collider can exclusively reveal The Serpent’s Vine, an adult dark fantasy graphic novel from GUNGNIR, created by Medney and co-written with The X-Files comics writer Stefan Petrucha. Illustrated by Bobby Raneshigue and Matteo Gennai, the book puts Adam and Eve in the middle of a dispute involving two other figures, Atticus and Luce. They disagree over humanity’s place in creation, and each has ambitions that reach well beyond the garden. GUNGNIR published the hardcover on November 17.

It has been revealed that four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

According to recent reports, you would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

Atticus and Luce give Medney and Petrucha room to ask a question that interested them about the original story. If human beings could make a disastrous choice in Eden, what was stopping the powers that created them from making one first? “What if paradise wasn’t perfect? What if the gods were just as flawed as the people they created?” Medney said in a statement shared with Collider.

“The idea that really drove this story was that death created scarcity, scarcity created inspiration, and inspiration gave birth to creativity.”.

In a recent development, for Petrucha, that invitation came thirty years after he explored a Gnostic version of Genesis in 1996’s The Bandy Man. This time, he scripted Medney’s story for Raneshigue and Gennai, whose artwork takes Eden from lush landscapes to scenes of graphic violence. Gennai also illustrated the cover, with Marcio Freire on colors, Dave Sharpe on letters, and Scarlet Witch writer Steve Orlando editing. Mohamed Samah contributed additional artwork and book design.

Industry observers note that the Serpent’s Vine is now available in hardcover from GUNGNIR, distributed by Macmillan, for $30 (USD)/$40 (CAD). Stay tuned at Collider for more.
